Newark Mayor Cory Booker Criticizes Republican Governor Chris Christie's Funding Cuts for Women's Health Services

At a Planned Parenthood rally in Charlotte, N.C., ahead of his Democratic National Convention speech, Newark Mayor Cory Booker made a statement criticizing Republican Governor Chris Christie's record on funding for women's health services. Booker implied that Christie's policies have denied women access to healthcare, without directly mentioning the governor's name.

According to a video posted on YouTube, Booker stated, "I come from a state where we've seen what Republican leadership will do to things like Planned Parenthood. We've seen it. The first budget that came out of our Republican leadership slashed funding to Planned Parenthood. It resulted in the reduction of hours, the elimination of days, elimination of access to women in my city and all over my state."

PolitiFact New Jersey investigated Booker's claim and found it to be accurate. In his first budget for fiscal year 2011, Christie eliminated nearly $7.5 million in funding for family planning services. This reduction in funding led to the closure of six family planning clinics across the state, including facilities operated by Planned Parenthood affiliates.

The clinics that closed included the Westampton and Brown Mills locations run by the Burlington County Health Department, Planned Parenthood of Southern New Jersey's Cherry Hill center, FamCare, Inc.'s Millville facility, the Bayonne Women's Health and Family Planning Center, and Planned Parenthood of Greater Northern New Jersey's Dover site. Representatives of these clinics previously stated that the state funding cuts forced the closures.

Christie has rejected three legislative efforts to restore the funding, including a bill vetoed in June 2010 and two line-item vetoes in June 2011 and June of this year. In his vetoes, Christie argued that New Jersey residents have access to comprehensive reproductive health care services at other sites and that the state cannot afford to provide duplicative funding for family planning centers.

PolitiFact New Jersey's ruling on Booker's statement is that it is True. The governor's elimination of nearly $7.5 million in funding for family planning services in the fiscal year 2011 budget, and his subsequent rejection of efforts to restore that funding, led to the closure of six family planning clinics around the state.

Health Care Reform Subsidies: Who Qualifies and How Much Do They Pay?

In the ongoing debate over health care reform, a crucial aspect of the legislation has received relatively little attention: the income threshold for federal health insurance subsidies. On March 21, 2010, Sen. Orrin Hatch, R-Utah, brought this issue to light during an interview on CNN's State of the Union, stating, "Do you realize they're going to subsidize families that make over -- families of four that make over $80,000 a year?"

To verify Hatch's claim, a review of the health care reform bill's provisions was conducted. The subsidies will become effective in 2014 and are designed for individuals who purchase insurance through virtual marketplaces, known as exchanges. These exchanges will serve people without employer-sponsored insurance and those not covered by government programs such as Medicare or Medicaid. The bill offers two types of subsidies: one for insurance premiums and another for out-of-pocket medical costs.

Under the premium subsidy, the government will cover the difference between the premiums for a designated plan and a set percentage of the individual's income. The cost-sharing subsidy aims to reduce the amount beneficiaries must pay for co-pays and other medical expenses. The subsidies will be available to individuals earning between 133 percent and 400 percent of the federal poverty level.

At the upper end of this income range, those earning 300 percent to 400 percent of the poverty level will qualify for premium subsidies. The government will cover the amount of the premium exceeding 9.5 percent of the beneficiary's income. For a family of four, the federal poverty limit is $22,050, and 400 percent of this amount would be $88,200.

Health care experts confirmed that $88,200 is indeed the top income threshold for receiving subsidies. This means that many individuals earning subsidies will have incomes above the median income for married couples, which is $73,010.

However, the purchasing power of $88,200 varies significantly depending on the location. In states with higher costs of living, such as New Jersey, Maryland, Connecticut, and Massachusetts, $88,200 is below the median income for a family of four. Conversely, in states with lower median incomes, such as Arkansas and Mississippi, $88,200 is well above the median.

The bill does not address geographic variations in income and cost of living. Furthermore, families making $88,200 will need to spend significantly before they become eligible for federal subsidies. The maximum amount an individual must pay for health insurance premiums before subsidies kick in is $8,379 (9.5 percent of $88,200).

Experts note that premiums above $8,000 are plausible, especially for older Americans not yet 65, who can enroll in Medicare at that age. Those aged 64 can be charged up to three times as much as an 18-year-old for the same coverage, making it unaffordable for families with older adults to purchase coverage without a subsidy.

In conclusion, while the health care reform bill will indeed provide subsidies to families making over $80,000 a year, the complexity of the legislation and the varying costs of living across the country must be considered. The subsidies will operate on a sliding scale, and the income threshold for receiving subsidies is $88,200 for a family of four.

Fox News host Sean Hannity recently stated that the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, a federal appeals court that hears cases from most of the western United States and Alaska and Hawaii, would likely rule against President Donald Trump's executive order on immigration. On February 9, a panel of three judges from the 9th Circuit unanimously ruled to affirm a decision by a federal trial court judge in Seattle, temporarily blocking the enforcement of the executive order.

The decision was part of a lawsuit filed by several states against the Trump administration, which had appealed the initial ruling to the 9th Circuit. The administration may choose to appeal the decision further to the Supreme Court, as President Trump tweeted after the ruling, "SEE YOU IN COURT, THE SECURITY OF OUR NATION IS AT STAKE!"

Hannity claimed that the 9th Circuit is the "most overturned court in the country," citing its reputation as a liberal court. However, a review of the court's reversal rate found that while it does have a higher-than-average reversal rate, it is not the highest among the circuit courts.

According to data from SCOTUSBlog, the Supreme Court has reversed about 70 percent of cases it took between 2010-2015. Among cases reviewed from the 9th Circuit, the Supreme Court reversed about 79 percent. However, this rate is not the highest, with the 6th Circuit having an 87 percent average reversal rate between 2010-2015.

Experts pointed out that the 9th Circuit's reversal rate may be influenced by its massive size, with over 12,000 cases filed in the 12 months leading up to March 2015. The Supreme Court only heard 11 cases from the 9th Circuit in 2015, reversing eight. This means that the Supreme Court generally reverses far less than 1 percent of all the cases the 9th Circuit decides.

University of Pennsylvania law professors Jonah Gelbach and Kermit Roosevelt noted that the sheer size of the 9th Circuit, as well as some of its procedures, may cause it to produce more "outlier decisions" that are reversed by the Supreme Court. However, they also stated that the 9th Circuit's reversal rate is not a reliable measure of the quality of its decisions.

In conclusion, while the 9th Circuit does have a higher-than-average reversal rate, it is not the highest among the circuit courts. The Supreme Court's reversal rate is influenced by various factors, including the size of the circuit and the complexity of the cases. As such, Hannity's claim that the 9th Circuit is the "most overturned court in the country" is not supported by the evidence.

New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie claimed to have unique experience in prosecuting terrorists during the first Republican presidential debate of the 2016 cycle. When debate moderator Megyn Kelly asked him about Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul's position on the National Security Agency's bulk collection of Americans' phone records, Christie invoked the worst terrorist attack on American soil in the country's history.

"I was appointed U.S. attorney by President Bush on Sept. 10, 2001, and the world changed enormously the next day, and that happened in my state," he said. Christie stated that this experience gave him a unique understanding of the PATRIOT Act, having "filed applications under the PATRIOT Act" and "prosecuted and investigated and jailed terrorists in this country after Sept. 11."

Christie's comment started a back-and-forth with Paul, who spent more than 10 hours on the Senate floor in May protesting the PATRIOT Act. Christie characterized Paul's experience as: "sitting in a subcommittee, just blowing hot air about this...."

Christie's statement about becoming the U.S. attorney for New Jersey the day before 9/11 is similar to statements he's made while campaigning in New Hampshire. However, a closer examination of the facts reveals that Christie's nomination as U.S. attorney was announced nearly four months after the terrorist attacks.

According to a report published in the New York Times on Dec. 8, 2001, President George Bush announced he would nominate Christie as the next U.S. attorney for New Jersey on Dec. 7, 2001. A White House press release also stated that the president "intends to nominate" Christie as the next U.S. attorney for New Jersey on the same day.

Christie's campaign in New Hampshire clarified that the governor received a phone call on Sept. 10, 2001, from Attorney General John Ashcroft that set in motion a months-long hiring process. According to an article in New Jersey's Star-Ledger newspaper from Sept. 11, 2001, the White House notified Christie that he was the President's choice for U.S. attorney, and extensive background checks on his qualifications would begin immediately.

Christie was officially confirmed by the U.S. senate on Dec. 20, 2001, and sworn into office on Jan. 17, 2002. Despite this, Christie unequivocally stated twice that he was appointed on Sept. 10, giving the impression that he took the job as U.S. attorney the day before the terrorist attacks and then "prosecuted and investigated and jailed terrorists in this country after Sept. 11."

However, the word "appoint" has multiple meanings, including "to name officially" or "to fix or set officially." While Christie's interpretation may be technically correct, his statement was misleading to viewers, suggesting that he was in charge of prosecuting and investigating terrorists immediately following the 9/11 attacks.

Our ruling
Christie said, "I was appointed U.S. attorney by President Bush on Sept. 10, 2001, and the world changed enormously the next day, and that happened in my state." However, his statement contains an element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression, so we rate the statement Mostly False.

On NBC's Meet the Press, former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, R-Ga., pointed to a labor statistic as evidence that the economy continues to face challenges more than five years after the onset of the last recession. 

Gingrich argued that the implementation of President Barack Obama's health care law could push some companies to convert full-time workers into part-timers in order to avoid providing health coverage. He expressed concern that this would lead to a significant increase in the number of people working part-time who would prefer to work full-time, as well as those who have stopped looking for work.

To support his argument, Gingrich cited the U-6 number, a federal statistic that measures labor-market weakness by taking into account not just people who are unemployed but also those working part-time who would prefer full-time work and those who have stopped looking for work. According to Gingrich, the U-6 number rose to 13.5 percent.

However, experts say that while the U-6 number did rise, the increase was not statistically significant. The seasonally adjusted figure for April 2013 was 13.9 percent, up from 13.8 percent in March. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a change of one-tenth of a percentage point is not considered statistically significant.

Moreover, the U-6 number has been trending downward since its peak in April 2010, with the exception of April 2013. Since January 2013, the statistic has fallen by half a percentage point, which is statistically significant.

Economists interviewed for this article agree that labor market measures have improved significantly from their weakest point in 2010, but acknowledge that conditions are still historically high. George Washington University economist Tara Sinclair noted that key measurements are "still historically very high and not dropping precipitously," particularly this long after the beginning of the last recession.

Gary Burtless, a senior fellow with the Brookings Institution, stated that while conditions are improving way too slowly, the April employment report does not contain evidence of a weakening in the trend toward a better job market. He pointed out that the number of payroll jobs increased by 165,000 in April and has increased 635,000 since January.

In conclusion, while Gingrich is correct that the U-6 number rose, the increase was not statistically significant and has been outweighed by a consistent decline in the numbers over the past three years. Therefore, we rate his claim Half True.

In an interview with former President Bill Clinton on ABC's This Week on April 18, 2010, host Jake Tapper discussed Clinton's experience with Supreme Court nominations, particularly that of Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who was confirmed in the Senate with a 96-3 vote in 1993. Tapper noted that Sen. Orrin Hatch, a senior Republican on the Senate Judiciary Committee, credited Clinton with involving him in the consultation process when Ginsburg was chosen.

Tapper asked Clinton for advice on how President Obama could navigate the current political environment, where Republicans are claiming that he is not including them in the process. Clinton began by explaining that he faced a different political landscape during his presidency.

"Well, I think for one thing, I had to do a little more of that (reaching out to Republicans) because I never had a filibuster-proof Senate," Clinton said. "And now there are 41 of them, although I think that a lot of those who come from more progressive states, the two Maine senators, the new senator from Massachusetts, a lot of them may think they already gave it the store on the health care deal or whatever they're doing on financial reform. I think it will be very difficult to just outright block a Supreme Court nominee that's otherwise qualified."

The discussion highlighted the importance of political ratios in the legislative process, particularly in the context of the close votes on health care reform. To assess Clinton's claim that he never had a filibuster-proof Senate, researchers looked into the Senate's composition during his presidency.

A filibuster is an attempt by the minority party to block a vote on an issue, requiring a three-fifths majority (60 out of 100 senators) to invoke cloture and overcome a filibuster. When Clinton came into office in 1993, Democrats held a majority in the Senate, but the ratio was not filibuster-proof. Senate records show that Republicans held 43 seats when Clinton took office, and they added another seat in June of that year with the election of Kay Bailey Hutchison, R-Texas.

The Senate breakdown when Clinton nominated Ginsburg on June 14, 1993, was 56 Democrats to 44 Republicans, which was the closest Clinton would come to having a filibuster-proof Senate. However, Republicans won a majority of seats in the Senate in the 1994 elections and retained control of both houses throughout the remainder of Clinton's presidency.

The party split resurfaced later in the interview when Tapper asked Clinton a question similar to one posed to his wife, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who championed the health care reform bill in 1993 and 1994. Both Clintons were asked if they felt that their efforts on health care had paved the way for Obama's success.

Hillary Clinton said she did not feel that way, stating that she was delighted the bill passed and that it was "a long time coming." Bill Clinton, on the other hand, said he "absolutely" felt that their efforts had laid the groundwork for Obama's success.

Clinton explained that his health plan ultimately failed because he couldn't pass it without the support of five or six Republicans, whereas Obama had an advantage with a clear filibuster-proof majority, at least for his first year. This is one issue where Clinton faced difficulty due to the lack of a filibuster-proof majority.

After conducting research, it was determined that Clinton's statement about not having a filibuster-proof Senate was accurate.

David Stockman, the former budget director for President Ronald Reagan, and Rep. Mike Pence, a conservative Indiana Republican and potential presidential candidate, engaged in a discussion on the topic of taxes and deficits on the show "This Week with Christiane Amanpour." The debate centered on whether raising taxes or letting the deficit run wild is more detrimental to the country.

Stockman argued that the deficit poses a significant threat to the country and criticized the Republican Party for its reluctance to consider tax increases. He stated that the party's refusal to address spending has led to the current massive deficit, which will ultimately end in disaster. Pence, on the other hand, agreed that Republicans had allowed spending to increase during the George W. Bush administration but emphasized that the party is now more committed to reducing government spending.

Pence proposed a plan to freeze domestic spending at pre-stimulus levels, which would save $100 billion in the first year. He also suggested implementing a net hiring freeze on Capitol Hill and reforming entitlement programs such as Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security. Stockman countered that these measures are not sufficient and that drastic cuts to Medicare and defense spending are necessary. He also emphasized the need to raise revenue through tax increases.

Pence disputed Stockman's assertion that tax increases would generate more revenue, citing historical data from the IRS that suggests raising income tax rates can actually reduce federal revenues. However, fact-checkers consulted the data and found that Pence's claim is not supported by the evidence.

Experts from various organizations, including the nonpartisan Tax Policy Center and the conservative Heritage Foundation, were consulted to examine the relationship between tax rates and tax revenues. They concluded that, at current tax rates, most tax increases would increase revenues, at least in the short and medium run.

The Treasury Department's 2006 report on the revenue effects of major tax law changes since World War II also contradicts Pence's claim. The report found that tax laws that reduced tax rates produced declines in revenues, while those that increased tax rates produced increases in tax revenues.

Stockman agreed with Pence's underlying assumption that increases in taxes can inhibit economic growth but disagreed that tax revenues would decrease if the government raised taxes. Experts consulted by fact-checkers also agreed with Stockman, stating that raising the top tax rates from 35 to 39.6 percent would increase revenues.

In conclusion, Pence's statement that raising income tax rates will likely reduce federal revenues is not supported by the evidence. Experts and historical data suggest that, at current tax rates, most tax increases would increase revenues, at least in the short and medium run.

White stated, "In Rick Perry's Texas, the governor threatens to leave, to secede from the greatest country in the world." 

According to White's spokeswoman, Katy Bacon, White was referring to a 2009 incident where Perry spoke at a tea-party rally outside Austin's city hall. Perry's comments were in response to a question from an Associated Press reporter, Kelley Shannon, about whether the gathering reflected a national movement. Perry replied that it could be, citing people's feelings of being "strangled by spending and taxation" and their desire for help.

Shannon then asked Perry about some associating him with the idea of secession or sovereignty for Texas. Perry responded by mentioning that when Texas entered the union in 1845, one of the issues was the state's potential to leave if it decided to do so. He stated, "You know, my hope is that America and Washington in particular pays attention. We've got a great union. There is absolutely no reason to dissolve it. But if Washington continues to thumb their nose at the American people, you know, who knows what may come out of that?"

Levinson stated that neither the Texas Constitution, the U.S. Constitution, nor the Joint Resolution Annexing Texas to the United States of 1845 explicitly granted the state the right to return to a republic.

The question remains as to whether Perry's comment about "who-knows-what-might-come" supports White's statement that Perry threatened to leave the union. A search of major newspaper articles found that none quoted Perry as threatening to push for secession, although critics and comedians framed his words in that way. Some experts and journalists interpreted Perry's comments as an attempt to point a critical finger at the federal government rather than encouraging secession.

In conclusion, while Perry's comments in 2009 were seen as a saber-rattling threat, he has not said that Texas should quit the United States. White's statement at the party's convention has been disputed as False.

A widely shared image on Facebook claims to show a dramatic increase in the number of vaccinations recommended for children over the years. The image lists the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) recommended vaccinations for children, stating that the number of vaccines went from three shots in 1962 to more than 50 in 2019.

The image has been shared in conjunction with a claim that the 1986 National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act was responsible for the increase in recommended vaccinations. However, this claim misrepresents the law and its relationship to the CDC's current vaccine schedule.

The 1986 National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act was enacted to address concerns about vaccine liability and ensure the nation's access to vaccines. The law established the National Vaccine Program Office, the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS), and the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program. It also required healthcare workers to provide information to patients about the risks and benefits of vaccines.

Contrary to the claim, the CDC's vaccination schedule is updated annually in response to health issues impacting the U.S. and as new vaccines become available. The schedule has undergone changes over the years, with the addition of new vaccines such as the hepatitis B vaccine, chickenpox vaccine, and rotavirus vaccine.

According to Seth Mnookin, author of "The Panic Virus: The True Story Behind the Vaccine-Autism Controversy," the claim that the U.S. has become "sicker and sicker" due to vaccines is unfounded. Multiple large-scale studies have found no association between childhood vaccines and poor health or chronic conditions.

The CDC's current vaccination schedule for children from birth to 18 years old lists 12 vaccines, which provide protection against 16 diseases and are administered in up to 54 shots, including boosters and annual flu shots.

In conclusion, the claim that the 1986 National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act led to a dramatic increase in recommended vaccinations is false. The law was enacted to address concerns about vaccine liability and ensure access to vaccines, and the CDC's vaccination schedule is updated annually in response to health issues and new vaccines.

Georgia's HOPE Scholarship Program Faces Funding Challenges

The HOPE scholarship program, a flagship initiative in Georgia, has been a vital source of financial aid for the state's top-performing students. However, the program's funding has been reduced in recent years, prompting concerns about its long-term sustainability.

In 2011, lawmakers implemented cuts to HOPE in an effort to rein in spending. As a result, the scholarship now provides less money to students, with only about 10 percent of recipients receiving full tuition coverage. The remaining recipients receive scholarships that cover 90 percent of tuition at 2010-11 academic year rates. Tuition rates have continued to rise, and the percentage of tuition covered by HOPE will likely decrease over time.

According to a statement made by the head of the state's flagship university, the HOPE scholarship program remains one of the most generous in the country. However, this assertion requires context. While Georgia's HOPE program was the largest and most generous of its kind in the past, its ranking may have changed in recent years due to funding cuts.

Data from the National Association of State Student Grant and Aid Programs (NASSGAP) provides insight into the program's relative generosity. In the 2008-09 school year, Georgia awarded nearly $567 million in total grant aid, ranking fourth in the nation behind California, New York, and Florida. When adjusted for the number of students enrolled in undergraduate programs, Georgia ranked second only to South Carolina.

However, NASSGAP's latest data, which dates back to the 2009-2010 academic year, shows that Georgia's HOPE program may no longer be the richest in the country. The state awarded about $672 million in non-needs-based scholarships, including HOPE, during this period. While this amount is still significant, it is lower than the $1 billion awarded by California in needs-based financial aid during the same year.

Projected funding for HOPE in the 2011-2012 academic year is approximately $590 million, which would likely place the program in the top five nationally. However, this ranking may be subject to change as other states adjust their funding levels in response to economic conditions.

In conclusion, while the HOPE scholarship program remains a vital source of financial aid for Georgia's top-performing students, its funding has been reduced in recent years. While the program may no longer be the richest in the country, it is likely to remain one of the most generous in the nation.

Misinformation Spreads on Social Media Ahead of Biden Certification

Supporters of President Donald Trump are set to gather in Washington D.C. to protest Congress officially certifying President-elect Joe Biden's victory. In the midst of this event, false information has emerged on social media regarding the city's mayor, Muriel Bowser.

A Facebook post claims that Bowser has ordered the closure of various businesses, including hotels, restaurants, and grocery stores, from January 4th to 6th, allegedly to discourage Trump supporters from gathering in D.C. The post advises supporters to bring extra supplies and have a plan for accommodations.

However, this claim has been flagged by Facebook as part of its efforts to combat false news and misinformation on its platform. In reality, Bowser has used her executive powers to implement measures to curb activities in the city, but these actions were taken on December 18 in response to a surge in COVID-19 cases, not in response to Trump supporters.

The order issued by Bowser advises residents to limit their activities to essential needs, including work, school, childcare, and medical services. It also closed indoor restaurant dining, museums, and libraries, while allowing outdoor dining and take-out services to continue.

Contrary to the Facebook post, the order does not mention the closure of hotels, grocery stores, gas stations, or convenience stores. However, Bowser has previously ordered that all businesses selling food must enforce physical distancing guidelines.

At least one hotel has chosen to close voluntarily during the specified dates. Hotel Harrington, which has been described as a popular spot for the Proud Boys, announced on December 28 that it would not accommodate guests except for long-term residents during that time period.

Bowser has directed the city's Homeland Security and Emergency Management Agency to help coordinate a response to demonstrations in D.C. In a statement issued on January 3, she asked Washington residents to stay out of the downtown area and avoid engaging with demonstrators who may be seeking confrontation. Officials will take necessary measures to ensure a peaceful environment for all attendees.

Many restaurants and office buildings in downtown D.C. have boarded up, a precautionary measure taken in response to previous demonstrations, including those related to racial justice and the presidential election, as reported by USA Today.

We rate this Facebook post as False.

Ohio Governor Ted Strickland's re-election campaign has maintained a consistent message that his Republican opponent, John Kasich, contributed to job losses in the state through his support of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) and other overseas trade deals, particularly with China.

However, an examination of the EPI study and other relevant data reveals that calculating job losses and gains is a complex issue that cannot be reduced to simple numbers. The EPI study estimated job losses based on "displaced production" resulting from trade imbalances, rather than actual job losses.

The General Accounting Office has noted that job losses attributed to NAFTA may have been overestimated, as some imports displaced imports from other countries rather than domestic production. Additionally, the Congressional Budget Office and the Congressional Research Service have concluded that factors other than NAFTA contributed to the widening trade deficit with Mexico.

Similarly, the estimate of jobs lost to China is also subject to significant limitations. The figure comes from a recent EPI study, which is based on the same methodology as the NAFTA study. However, other economic policies and forces, such as product dumping, price controls, and currency manipulation, have also affected the trade imbalance with China, making it difficult to isolate the impact of normalized trade relations.

Kasich did vote in favor of NAFTA and normalizing trade relations with China, but labeling these agreements as "Kasich's trade deals" is an oversimplification, as they received support from both Democrats and Republicans.

In conclusion, the Strickland campaign's claims about job losses are based on studies that did not actually count lost jobs and are subject to numerous limitations and complexities. Therefore, we rate Strickland's claim as False.

For a decade, Republicans in Madison have been waiting for their chance to impose a photo ID requirement on Wisconsin's elections. Now, with power in their grasp, they've crafted a bill that critics warn will decimate voter access.

Opponents, including members of the Milwaukee Common Council, are sounding the alarm. Ald. In contrast, Florida accepts 12 different forms of ID, including employee badges and public assistance cards. Hawaii is even more lenient, requiring only a signed picture ID.

The debate is heating up, with opponents questioning whether Wisconsin should accept student IDs. Many students lack a Wisconsin driver's license, and critics wonder if they'll be motivated to get a state ID before voting. Republicans are resisting calls to allow student IDs, citing concerns about fraud and administrative headaches.

But the evidence suggests otherwise. David Canon, a University of Wisconsin political scientist, agrees with Coggs that Wisconsin's bill is the most restrictive. Kevin Kennedy, the state's elections chief, also warns that the bill will have a disproportionate impact on vulnerable populations.

As the bill stands, it's clear that Wisconsin's Republicans are determined to limit voter access. But will they listen to critics and expand the list of accepted IDs? Michael Pyritz, a GOP staff expert, predicts that lawmakers will eventually allow the use of passports and tribal IDs. But for now, the bill remains a draconian measure that threatens the very fabric of our democracy.

Constables in Texas Face Risks in the Line of Duty

Constables in Texas often face risks while carrying out their duties, according to Bruce Elfant, the constable for Precinct 5 in Travis County. Elfant stated that constables serve as the enforcement arm for Texas courts, executing court orders, arresting individuals, and enforcing child-support orders, among other responsibilities. He noted that constables frequently encounter hostility, resistance, and, in some cases, deadly force.

In a statement made on August 13, 2012, Elfant mentioned that 88 Texas constables have died in the line of duty while serving their communities. However, when asked to provide evidence to support this claim, Elfant admitted to miscounting and said he based his figure on a tally of 86 constables that was part of a video about constables posted on the Travis County website.

Further investigation revealed that the original count of 86 constables came from a list compiled by Ron Hickman, the constable in Harris County's Precinct 4. The list, which included information from the Combined Law Enforcement Associations of Texas, showed that 215 constables or officers in constable offices in approximately 100 counties have died in the line of duty since October 17, 1852. This total includes 150 constables.

The list showed that the majority of deaths occurred in the 1800s and early 1900s, with a significant number of deaths due to gunfire. More recent research, however, suggests that the total number of constable deaths may be higher.

A spokesperson for the Combined Law Enforcement Associations of Texas, Charley Wilkison, explained that the group's members have helped spearhead the creation of the Texas Peace Officers' Memorial and have undertaken research efforts to confirm officers who died in the line of duty. Volunteer retired police officers have combed through libraries and cemeteries to verify the information.

The Texas Commission on Law Enforcement Standards and Education, which maintains the memorial, reported that as of May 2011, 85 constables were shown as having died in the line of duty. However, this count is likely not complete.

After comparing the lists, researchers found that at least 30 constables on the non-government list had yet to be approved to appear on the memorial, and another 30 constables whose names are on the memorial were not shown on the state's list. Additionally, some officers on the memorial were identified as deputy sheriffs but were also constables.

The agency's legislative liaison, Ken Mobley, stated that it is reasonable to say that at least 115 Texas constables have died in the line of duty, and the total could be higher.

Ultimately, our investigation found that while the exact number of constable deaths is unclear, there is agreement between the agency that oversees the Capitol memorial and outside researchers that the total is at least 115 deaths, not 88, as initially stated by Elfant.

Georgia School Funding: State's Share Decreases, But Officials Dispute Claim of Drastic Cuts

For the first time in more than a decade, federal officials report that local school systems are contributing a larger percentage of public education funding than state governments. This shift has led to a reevaluation of the state's role in education spending.

Georgia state officials have disputed claims that the state has drastically cut education spending. Senator Fran Millar, chairman of the Georgia Senate's Education and Youth Committee, stated that the state has reduced funding for education the least, with education spending on children from kindergarten to the 12th grade not dramatically declining in recent years.

However, PolitiFact Georgia examined Millar's statement to determine its accuracy. According to data from the Georgia Office of Planning and Budget, the state's current 12-month spending plan for k-12 education is approximately $7.2 billion, which is about 38% of the state's current $19 billion fiscal year budget.

Millar attributed his statement to the percentage of spending on education, as it is a significant portion of state spending. He emphasized that the state had not made drastic cuts in education spending, stating that it was "the least-touched major area" in terms of cuts.

Recent budget cuts have affected various state departments, with Gov. Nathan Deal and his budget staff asking departments to come up with an additional $553 million in budget cuts by the 2014 budget cycle. However, the major portion of public school funding is exempt from these cuts.

PolitiFact Georgia examined state spending since Deal took office in 2011 and from 2009, the year after the Great Recession began making an impact on state and local budgets. The data revealed that education spending has remained relatively stable, with a slight increase of 1.1% between FY 2011 and the current budget.

A breakdown of education spending in recent fiscal years shows:

- FY 2009: $8.20 billion
- FY 2010: $6.59 billion
- FY 2011: $7.07 billion
- FY 2012: $6.97 billion
- FY 2013: $7.17 billion

Comparing education spending to other large departments, PolitiFact Georgia found that the Education Department's budget rose by slightly more than 1% between FY 2011 and the current budget. This increase was the smallest among the 10 departments with the largest budgets.

Between FY 2011 and FY 2012, the Education Department's budget declined by slightly more than 1%, which was the smallest decrease among the 10 departments. Five departments had budget increases, some as high as about 15%, as was the case for the Department of Community Health.

Since FY 2009, the Education Department's budget declined by 12.5%, which was a smaller decrease than several other departments with large budgets. The Corrections Department was the only one with a smaller decrease, which was about 3%.

Senator Millar countered that the state had no choice but to increase spending in some areas, such as the Department of Community Health, which oversees Georgia's Medicaid program. State officials estimate they'll have to spend about $4 billion in coming years to comply with the federal health care law.

In conclusion, while Millar's statement that the state has not made major cuts in education spending is supported by some data, other findings suggest that the state's education spending has not been entirely immune to budget cuts. PolitiFact Georgia rates Millar's claim Half True, as it is partially accurate but also subject to some nuance.

Rhode Island's Gambling Revenue Continues to Rise Amid Economic Slump

Despite a sluggish economy, Rhode Island's gambling revenue has been steadily increasing. According to a recent report, the state's gambling industry generated approximately $355 million in revenue during the 2011 fiscal year, making it the state's third-largest source of revenue.

However, not everyone is pleased with the state's reliance on gambling revenue. The Rev. Eugene J. McKenna, president of Citizens Concerned About Casino Gambling, expressed concerns that the social costs of gambling far outweigh the financial benefits for the state. He claimed that Rhode Island receives more revenue per capita from gambling than any other state in the country.

PolitiFact Rhode Island investigated this claim to determine its validity. We asked Father McKenna to provide evidence to support his statement, but he cited a 2006 report by the National Conference on State Legislatures and a 2008 report by the Tax Foundation. However, upon further examination, we found that these reports had significant flaws.

The National Conference on State Legislatures report ranked Rhode Island second behind West Virginia in terms of gambling revenue per capita, but the comparison was flawed because Rhode Island reported only gross sales, while other states reported net sales figures. The Tax Foundation report, which ranked Rhode Island at the top of its list, analyzed only lottery sales per capita and did not account for revenues from other sources of gambling.

In search of more accurate information, we consulted a study by the Nelson A. Rockefeller Institute of Government, which examined the four major types of legalized gambling and calculated revenues on a per-adult basis. According to the 2011 report, Rhode Island's total gambling revenue, including lottery sales, slot parlors, and other betting, totaled approximately $346 million in the 2010 fiscal year.

Using the Rockefeller Institute's calculation, which compared revenues per adult resident, we found that Rhode Island's gambling revenue per adult was approximately $418, making it the highest in the nation. Nevada ranked second with $407 per adult, and Delaware came in third with $397.

In conclusion, while the initial reports cited by Father McKenna were flawed, the Rockefeller Institute's comprehensive study provided a more accurate picture of Rhode Island's gambling revenue. Therefore, we rule his statement True.

The debate over marijuana has gained momentum in Wisconsin, with Gov. Tony Evers proposing the legalization of recreational and medical marijuana in the 2021-23 state budget. According to Evers, legalizing marijuana would ensure safe products are available to users while providing a new source of revenue for rural schools and programs for marginalized communities.

Wisconsin is one of a minority of states that have not legalized marijuana for medical or recreational use. However, the proposal has already faced opposition from Republicans, who have rejected similar efforts in the past. State Sen. Chris Kapenga, R-Delafield, expressed concerns about the potential risks associated with marijuana use, citing a correlation between marijuana and psychotic disorders, particularly in teenagers.

In a tweet, Kapenga stated that the National Academy of Medicine points to a significant correlation between marijuana and psychosis, schizophrenia, and other psychotic disorders, particularly in teenagers where the risk of developing schizophrenia increases threefold. However, State Sen. Melissa Agard countered with the claim that youth usage of marijuana has actually decreased in states that have fully legalized it.

To examine Kapenga's claim, researchers looked into the relationship between marijuana and psychotic disorders. According to the National Institute of Mental Health, people experiencing psychosis have lost some contact with reality and can exhibit hallucinations or delusions. A 2017 report by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine found "substantial evidence" that marijuana use can increase the risk of developing schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders, particularly among frequent users.

However, the report also noted that people with schizophrenia or other psychoses and a history of marijuana use may perform better on cognitive learning and memory tasks. A separate 2019 study in Europe found that the odds of a psychotic disorder increased among daily marijuana users, particularly among those using strains with a higher THC content.

Regarding the impact on youth, researchers have found that people who start smoking marijuana regularly before age 14 have a 2 to 3 times greater risk of developing schizophrenia or a psychotic disorder. A 2002 study in New Zealand found that a tenth of cannabis users by age 15 developed schizophreniform disorder by age 26, compared to 3% of the remaining cohort. Another study found that 15 and 16-year-olds who tried marijuana were more likely to exhibit three or more early symptoms of psychosis, even when researchers controlled for previous behavioral symptoms.

In light of this research, Daniel Yohanna, an associate professor of psychiatry at the University of Chicago, stated that the earlier people start smoking marijuana and the more they smoke, the greater their risk of developing schizophrenia. Based on this evidence, it appears that Kapenga's claim is supported.

Our analysis concludes that there is extensive research showing a correlation between marijuana use and psychotic disorders, particularly among frequent users and those who start using marijuana at a young age. Therefore, we rate Kapenga's claim as True.

U.S. Rep. Connie Mack IV, R-Fort Myers, has made a revised claim about his Senate opponent, Democrat Bill Nelson, regarding his voting record on taxes. Mack initially stated that Nelson voted to raise taxes 150 times, but in a recent fundraising email, he corrected the number to 272 times.

The Mack campaign claims that this revised number includes votes from Nelson's time in the Florida House of Representatives (1973-78) and the U.S. House of Representatives (1979-90). However, a fact-check by PolitiFact has raised questions about the accuracy of this claim.

Upon reviewing the Mack campaign's list, PolitiFact found that about half of the initial 150 votes were Democratic budget resolutions, which set non-binding parameters for considering tax and spending legislation. These resolutions do not technically change tax law, and it is debatable whether they should be counted as votes for higher taxes.

Furthermore, the Mack campaign's tally includes multiple votes on the same budget resolution and actual legislation. For example, Mack cites nine votes Nelson took in 2008 about Congressional Resolution 70, a five-year budget plan. This is an example of duplicative counting, which inflates the number of votes.

Additionally, the Mack campaign's definition of "higher taxes" is broad and includes votes against tax cuts as well as votes to raise taxes. This could leave voters with a false impression, as opposing a tax cut is not necessarily the same as voting to raise taxes.

PolitiFact also noted that Nelson has sometimes voted in favor of tax cuts, including extending tax cuts in 2006 and 2010. In 2010, he supported keeping tax cuts for those earning less than $250,000, and in 2006, he supported extending tax cuts.

The Mack campaign's revised claim includes Nelson's votes from the Florida House and the U.S. House of Representatives, as well as some obscure or non-binding votes. Many of these votes were about fees or only applied to a portion of the state's taxpayers.

After reviewing the Mack campaign's list, PolitiFact found that about 18 of the U.S. House votes cited by Mack were non-binding resolutions, and there were about 38 duplicative votes. The campaign also included some key House votes of Nelson in favor of higher taxes, which were confirmed by PolitiFact.

In conclusion, while Nelson did take some votes that raised taxes, the Mack campaign's revised claim of 272 votes for higher taxes is an exaggeration. PolitiFact rates this claim False, citing the inclusion of duplicative votes, non-binding resolutions, and obscure or non-binding votes that do not accurately reflect Nelson's voting record on taxes.

Florida Democrats Released a Web Video Criticizing Governor Rick Scott's Record on Corruption.

The Florida Democratic Party released a web video aimed at criticizing Governor Rick Scott's record on corruption, specifically highlighting a report by Integrity Florida that ranked Florida as the state with the most government corruption convictions between 2000 and 2010. The video features a clip of Scott saying, "Florida won't stop until we're No. 1," followed by a newspaper headline stating, "Study ranks Florida No. 1 in government corruption."

However, the video's claim is based on a study that was released in 2012, prior to Scott's inauguration. The report by Integrity Florida specifically noted that the data was from a time period prior to Scott's taking office, in an effort to discourage any correlation between Scott and the corruption cases.

The Florida Republican Party has taken issue with the video, arguing that it misrepresents the facts. Integrity Florida's executive director, Dan Krassner, stated that the organization was concerned about the interpretation of the report, which was intended to highlight the state's corruption issues prior to Scott's tenure.

The Florida Democratic Party, however, stands by the video, citing a lack of progress on ethics reform by Scott's administration. Spokesman Joshua Karp pointed to a story by the Tampa Bay Times/Miami Herald about Scott's failure to follow through on ethics reform promises.

It is worth noting that while Florida was ranked as the state with the most government corruption convictions between 2000 and 2010, the state is not universally considered the most corrupt. A separate study by researchers at the University of Illinois at Chicago found that Florida ranked No. 4 in total federal public corruption convictions over a broader time period, and No. 8 per capita.

In conclusion, the video's claim that Florida is No. 1 in government corruption is misleading, as the report specifically noted that the data was from a time period prior to Scott's taking office. The video does not provide a complete picture of Scott's record on corruption, and the Democratic Party's interpretation of the report is overly broad.

U.S. Rep. Matt Cartwright's Republican Challenger Misrepresents Cartwright's Stance on Police Funding

A recent news release from the Jim Bognet for Congress campaign accused U.S. Rep. Matt Cartwright of supporting the "defund the police" movement, a claim that Cartwright's campaign disputes. The statement, made in a June 12 email, alleged that Cartwright proposes to defund the Wilkes-Barre police department.

However, an examination of the issue reveals that Cartwright does not support defunding the police. During a virtual listening session hosted by Cartwright in May with the Black Scranton Project and the Wilkes-Barre and Monroe County chapters of the NAACP, a participant asked whether he supports calls to defund the police. Cartwright responded that he personally does not agree with defunding and disbanding police forces.

Instead, Cartwright advocated for new investment in law enforcement officer training and an expansion of community policing. An audio clip of the exchange is available on Cartwright's Facebook page. The congressman also stated that the idea of defunding the police is not something he supports.

The Bognet campaign linked to another audio clip of the same virtual listening session, where a participant asked Cartwright if there's a way to reallocate funds from the Wilkes-Barre police department. Cartwright replied that public officials have the power to decide how public funds are spent on the police, as for any other public agency. This response was taken out of context by the Bognet campaign to support their claim that Cartwright wants to defund the Wilkes-Barre police department.

A spokesperson for the Bognet campaign interpreted Cartwright's response as evidence that he wants to defund the police, while a spokesperson for Cartwright's campaign stated that the congressman's response was about the process of deciding how to spend taxpayer money.

In conclusion, the Bognet campaign's statement that Cartwright proposes to defund the Wilkes-Barre police is false. Cartwright has explicitly stated that he does not agree with the idea of defunding the police and supports investing in law enforcement officer training and community policing.

Virginia Senate Kills Paid Family Leave Bill, But Committee Expresses Interest in Alternative Plan

A bill that would have established a paid family leave program for Virginia employees has been defeated in the state Senate. The legislation, introduced by Senator Jennifer Boysko (D-Fairfax), aimed to create a wage tax to finance up to 12 weeks of annual paid leave time for workers at 80% of their regular earnings.

The proposed program would have covered employees caring for a new child in the first year after birth, adoption, or foster placement, as well as those experiencing or caring for a family member with serious health problems, and those caring for the family of a deployed service member.

During a January 18 hearing of the Senate Commerce and Labor Committee, Senator Boysko stated that the bill would make Virginia a national leader on the issue of paid family leave. She noted that the United States is one of the few industrialized countries without a paid family medical leave program in place.

The United States currently has the Family and Medical Leave Act, which requires employers with 50 or more workers to allow parents 12 weeks of job-protected leave annually to care for a newborn. However, this leave is typically unpaid.

Several states, including California, New Jersey, Rhode Island, New York, Washington, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and Oregon, as well as the District of Columbia, offer paid family leave through employee-paid payroll taxes. Additionally, some employers provide paid maternity leave, but this benefits only about 16% of private industry workers, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

A study by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development found that, on average, mothers in developed countries are entitled to 51 weeks of paid leave after childbirth. The United States is the only country in the study with no national law providing this benefit.

The Senate committee ultimately voted 12-3 against the bill, citing concerns about the unclear definition of the wage tax and the potential financial hardships it could impose on small businesses and workers. However, the Senate has expressed interest in exploring alternative solutions, passing a bill that instructs the State Corporation Commission to make recommendations for establishing a plan that would encourage Virginia employers to voluntarily offer 12 weeks of paid family leave.

The measure is pending in the House of Delegates.

A federal judge has ordered the restoration of in-person early voting for the three days before election day in Ohio, following a federal lawsuit. The ruling comes as a result of efforts by the state's Republican-controlled legislature and GOP Secretary of State Jon Husted to reduce in-person early voting hours, citing budgetary concerns.

This move has been met with opposition from Democrats, including Rep. Marcia Fudge, who has claimed that Republicans are attempting to eliminate weekend early voting to cut turnout among African-American voters. However, Republicans have denied these allegations.

Fudge has pointed out that in Cuyahoga County, 56 percent of weekend voters in 2008 were African American, while adult African Americans comprise 28 percent of the county population. A recent study by Case Western Reserve University emeritus professor Norman Robbins and Cleveland State University urban affairs professor Mark Salling supports Fudge's claim.

The study found that in Cuyahoga County, 56.4 percent of early-in-person voters in 2008 were black, compared to 25.7 percent of those who voted on election day or by mail. The study also found that on the four weekends prior to election day, 56 percent of the ballots were cast by black voters.

In an email to PolitiFact Ohio, study co-author Robbins noted that African-American turnout was "disproportionately high and approximately the same, ranging from about 54 to 59 percent" during every early voting time period.

Cuyahoga County Election Board Director Jane Platten was unable to evaluate the study's statistics, citing the county's lack of data on voters' ethnicity. However, she did acknowledge that a significant number of African Americans made use of the county's early-in-person voting program.

The study's authors used voter addresses to determine the census block where voters reside and extrapolated their race by using 2010 census data on each block's racial makeup. This method was deemed valid by several independent demographics experts.

PolitiFact Ohio queried the Pew Research Center's survey research director, Scott Keeter, who noted that 2008 exit polling data in Ohio found that 16 percent of those who voted early were black voters, while 9 percent of in-person voters were black.

Fudge drew her statistics from a research study that stated that 56 percent of the 2008 Cuyahoga county voters who cast ballots on weekends before the election were African American. On the Truth-O-Meter, Fudge's claim rates True.

PolitiFact Oregon Investigates Oregon PTA's Claim on Class Size

A recent statement by the Oregon PTA has sparked interest in the state's class sizes. The group claimed that Oregon has the third-largest class size in the nation. PolitiFact Oregon decided to investigate this claim to determine its validity.

According to a 2013 report compiled by the National Education Association (NEA), the country's largest teacher union, Oregon was indeed ranked third in terms of student-teacher ratio, behind California and Utah. The NEA calculated this ranking based on the ratio of students to teachers.

However, it is essential to note that student-teacher ratio and class size are not exactly the same. Class size can be difficult to measure, as it varies depending on factors such as planning periods and students with special needs. Researchers often rely on staffing ratios to compare states, as there is a direct relationship between student-teacher ratio and class size.

Oregon's student-teacher ratio in the fall of 2011 was 20.2, according to the NEA. PolitiFact Oregon wanted to verify this information by checking other sources of data.

The state of Oregon calculates student-teacher ratios differently, using an average of full-time-equivalent teaching positions and student enrollment across the school year. The state's calculation resulted in a slightly higher number, with 21.3 students per teacher. This would still rank Oregon behind Utah and California in the NEA rankings.

To further verify the state's calculation, PolitiFact Oregon examined data from previous years. The statewide average student-teacher ratio was 19.1 in the 2008-2009 school year, and 18.9 according to the NEA. The United States Department of Education's database of school statistics also showed similar results, although not exactly matching the state numbers.

Overall, three data sets produced very similar results about Oregon's student-teacher ratios, indicating that the state has one of the highest student-teacher ratios in the United States. PolitiFact Oregon rates the statement as True.

House Republican Leader John Boehner Criticizes Omnibus Spending Bill with Thousands of Earmarks

On February 25, House Republican Leader John Boehner spoke on the House floor, expressing his disapproval of a spending bill containing approximately 9,000 earmarks. Boehner called on President Obama to veto the bill and instead support a version without pet projects.

Boehner stated that the president had campaigned against legislation with a high number of earmarks. However, several news organizations reported that Obama would sign the bill, earmarks and all, despite his campaign promises to reform the earmarking process. This claim was incorrect, as Obama had pledged to reform earmarks, eliminating wasteful or "screwy" projects.

A closer examination of Obama's campaign statements reveals that he did indeed make pledges to reform earmarks. In the first presidential debate, Obama stated that he would "go line by line" to ensure that earmarks were not spent unwisely. He also emphasized the need for increased transparency and accountability in the earmarking process.

In a statement on March 10, 2008, Obama said that the current earmarks process was flawed, as it often prioritized seniority over merit and allowed for wasteful spending. He also pledged to increase disclosure around earmarks and ensure that projects were not funded without public scrutiny.

A review of the omnibus spending bill reveals that it contains many earmarks that were added without transparency and may have been influenced by senior members of Congress. According to Keith Ashdown, investigator for Taxpayers for Common Sense, the earmarking process for the bill was not more transparent than it was during Obama's campaign. Additionally, seven of the top 10 earmark recipients in the Senate are on the Appropriations Committee, suggesting that access and seniority played a significant role in determining which projects received funding.

While the total cost of the earmarks in the bill is slightly less than the 1994 level, there were additional earmarks in previous spending bills passed last year. Ashdown noted that it is possible that there are wasteful projects in the bill, but he cautioned against making assumptions based on superficial appearances.

The White House has argued that Obama should not be held responsible for the earmarking process in this legislative package, as it is largely composed of bills that were supposed to be passed last year. However, this argument does not negate Boehner's point that the bill is the "type of legislation" Obama campaigned against, featuring earmarks added without transparency and pushing earmark spending well over the 1994 level.

In conclusion, Boehner's claim that the omnibus spending bill is the "type of legislation" Obama campaigned against is supported by evidence.

Austin Taxpayers Contribute to School Funding Elsewhere in the State

A system in place since the early 2000s allows the state to redistribute funds from wealthier school districts to those with less taxable property wealth. As a result, Austin taxpayers indirectly contribute to funding schools in other districts.

During a 2016 panel discussion, Democratic State Senator Kirk Watson mentioned that the average Austin homeowner pays approximately $1,300 to $1,400 in school property taxes towards recapture funds, which are shifted to less affluent districts. Watson emphasized the need for a fair and equitable school finance system.

The Austin Independent School District's chief financial officer, Nicole Conley, testified in 2016 that the district is the state's largest single payer of recapture funds. According to her prepared remarks, the district's payment alone accounts for 13% of all state collections. Between fiscal years 2016 and 2020, Austin ISD is projected to pay nearly $2.6 billion in recapture payments to the state.

Conley also stated that if the district were not sending $406 million to the state under the recapture system, it could lower its tax rate by 35 cents. This would result in approximately $1,400 in lower taxes for the average homeowner, making Austin more affordable for some taxpayers.

To calculate the average homeowner's share of the recapture payment, the district used its 2016-17 budget, which expected to pay $406 million in recapture to the state. This payment amounts to 38% of the district's $1.061 billion in budgeted property taxes. The district's average taxable value of a home is $328,844, and the owner of such a home is expected to pay $3,548 in school maintenance and operations property taxes at the M&O tax rate of $1.079 per $100 valuation.

Using this information, the district calculated that the average homeowner would pay $1,355 in school property taxes towards the district's recapture payment.

Experts from the Texas Education Agency, the Texas Association of School Business Officials, and a district advocate evaluated the district's calculation and found it to be solid. However, one expert cautioned that the average does not accurately describe the distribution of payment amounts, and it is unclear how many taxpayers are clustered close to the average amount and how many are far away.

To provide further context, the median value of homes in the Austin district as of August 8, 2016, is $261,487. Using the district's equation, a homeowner with a median-value home would be expected to pay $2,821 in M&O school taxes, of which $1,078 would be their share of the district's recapture payment.

Our analysis
The statement that the average Austin homeowner pays approximately $1,300 to $1,400 in school property taxes towards recapture funds is supported by the Austin Independent School District's calculation. We rate this claim True.

TRUE – The statement is accurate and there's nothing significant missing.

A Recent Claim About Hillary Clinton's Speaking Fees Has Been Questioned.

A recent Facebook post by the liberal group Occupy Democrats has been shared over 25,000 times, comparing Hillary Clinton's paid speeches to those given by former President George W. Bush. The post claims that Clinton has donated every cent she's ever earned from speaking fees to charity, while Bush keeps all of his speaking fees.

However, this claim is not entirely accurate. In 2014, Clinton stated that she had donated the fees from her university and college speeches to the Clinton Foundation. The Clinton Foundation's website confirms that the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, donated $225,000 to the foundation, which is listed as a contribution from the UNLV Foundation.

Upon further review, it appears that Clinton's comments were misinterpreted. Clinton's financial disclosure form, published by the New York Times in May, reveals that she received a total of 51 speech fees between January 2014 and March 2015, totaling over $11 million. This amount includes fees from various companies, as well as some university and college speeches.

The Clinton Foundation and Clinton's presidential campaign declined to comment on the matter. Our analysis shows that Occupy Democrats' claim is a misreading of Clinton's comments and does not accurately reflect her financial dealings.

In conclusion, the claim that Clinton has donated every cent she's ever earned from speaking fees to charity is false.

**ISIS Camp Claim Near El Paso Sparks Skepticism**

A conservative watchdog group, Judicial Watch, has claimed that a camp operated by the terrorist organization ISIS is located in Mexico, just a few miles from the U.S.-Mexico border in the city of Ciudad Juárez, which adjoins El Paso, Texas. According to Judicial Watch, the camp is situated approximately eight miles from the U.S. border in an area known as Anapra.

In a statement released on April 14, 2015, Judicial Watch cited anonymous sources, including a Mexican Army "field grade officer" and a Mexican Federal Police inspector, as confirming the presence of an ISIS camp in the region. The group also claimed that another ISIS cell was operating to the west of Ciudad Juárez, targeting the New Mexico towns of Columbus and Deming.

However, similar claims made by Judicial Watch in the past have not been substantiated. In September 2014, PolitiFact found no independent or law-enforcement corroboration of a statement that "ISIS is present in Ciudad Juárez." National security experts advised that it is unlikely ISIS would operate in Mexico and stage an attack by crossing the border.

When asked to elaborate on its claim, Judicial Watch stated that the two key sources were not authorized to speak on the record and that identifying them "would get them killed." The group's director of investigations and research, Christopher Farrell, maintained that Judicial Watch stands by its post.

Other authorities and government agencies have expressed skepticism regarding the claim. The National Security Council's spokesman, Alistair Baskey, stated that there is no indication that the claim has any validity. The FBI's El Paso-based spokesman, Michael Martinez, said that there is no credible information to support the claim. Mexico's embassy in Washington, D.C. also denied the claim, stating that "relevant authorities operating in the region have also confirmed the nonexistence of these activities with their U.S. counterparts."

The Texas Department of Public Safety and the El Paso County sheriff's office also expressed skepticism regarding the claim. Tom Vinger, spokesman for the Texas Department of Public Safety, stated that the agency has no credible information to corroborate or validate the story. Monica Varela, a public information officer for the El Paso County sheriff's office, expressed surprise and skepticism when informed of the claim.

Victor Manjarrez, a former U.S. Border Patrol official and associate director of the National Center for Border Security & Immigration at the University of Texas at El Paso, also expressed skepticism regarding the claim, stating that the described location of the camp is a suburb of Ciudad Juárez that is modern by Mexican standards.

PolitiFact has ruled the claim made by Judicial Watch as False, citing the lack of on-the-record indication of the claim's accuracy and the skepticism expressed by other authorities and government agencies.

**Rating: FALSE**

A State Official's Claim About Homeless Veterans Sparks Investigation

A recent statement by a Texas state official claiming that one-third of homeless men in the United States are veterans has been disputed by experts. The claim was made by Ericka Walmsley, a Texas Veterans Commission employment representative, in a news article published on December 5 in the Lubbock Avalanche-Journal.

According to Walmsley, "When their term is up and they get out, there's almost nothing for them now." She also cited a statistic from a Web page maintained by HelpUSA, a group that provides housing and supportive services for the homeless and those in need. The page states that "1 out of every 3 homeless men you see on the street is a veteran."

However, further investigation revealed that the statistic may be outdated. A chapter in a report posted online by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) states that "among homeless men, 33 percent report being veterans." But the report was published in 1996, and the data collection methods used at the time are no longer considered relevant.

When asked for clarification on the statistic, HUD officials pointed to more recent data. The HUD's Annual Homeless Assessment Report, which has been published since 2005, indicates that veterans accounted for 11 percent of the nation's 1.2 million sheltered homeless adults in 2009. This number is based on data collected from over 3,000 communities and represents a significant decrease from the 13 percent reported in 2007.

Neil Donovan, executive director of the National Coalition for the Homeless, confirmed that the 1-in-3 ratio is no longer accurate. He noted that the latest research indicates that veterans account for a smaller percentage of homeless men.

The U.S. Secretary of Veterans Affairs, Eric Shinseki, has also weighed in on the issue. In a speech delivered on December 7, Shinseki estimated the number of homeless veterans at 107,000, down from 131,000 two years earlier and 250,000 a decade ago.

In an effort to clarify the issue, this publication sought out additional information from experts in the field. A HUD public affairs officer, Brian Sullivan, explained that the 1-in-3 ratio is outdated and comes from a 1999 report that relied on data collected in 1996. He noted that the data collection methods used at the time are no longer considered relevant.

Dennis Culhane, a University of Pennsylvania professor who helped lead the latest HUD assessment, also confirmed that the 13 percent figure is a more accurate representation of the number of homeless veterans. "I cannot vouch for the (1-in-3) estimate and am not sure it was ever correct," he wrote in an email.

Mary Cunningham, a researcher who specializes in homeless issues for the Urban Institute, also cautioned that all numbers should be treated as rough estimates. She noted that there are far too many homeless veterans, regardless of the exact percentage.

In response to these findings, the Texas Veterans Commission has pointed to a March 2010 report by Project CHALENG, a federal effort to enhance the continuum of care for homeless veterans. The report suggests that homeless veterans are under-counted, but there are also fewer veterans overall. According to the report, the number of homeless veterans has decreased significantly over the past two decades.

In conclusion, while some experts agree that the 1-in-3 ratio may be justified based on certain data, the majority of experts outside Texas agree that the claim is based on outdated information. This publication rates the statement Barely True.

The Democratic Governors Association (DGA) has taken a particularly strong stance against Walker, releasing an online ad that claims he is "denying Democrats the right to vote."

The DGA's assertion is based on the state's new photo ID law for voting, which Walker signed in May 2011. Under the law, nearly all voters, with certain exceptions, must present photo identification beginning with the 2012 presidential primary election. Free ID cards are available from the state. Voters without a photo ID can cast a provisional ballot that will be counted if they show photo ID to an election clerk by the Friday after the election.

However, the DGA's evidence does not support the claim that Walker is denying Democrats the right to vote. The group's assertions are based on predictions that the photo ID law will lead some voters who tend to support Democrats to stop voting. While it is true that some residents may not have photo IDs, the law applies to all eligible voters, regardless of party affiliation.

The DGA also claims that the passage of the law was rushed and that voters in some Democratic areas of the state would find it more difficult to obtain a photo ID due to a plan by Walker to close some state Division of Motor Vehicles offices. However, the administration dropped the plan in August 2011, and the evidence cited by the DGA surfaced after the ad began running.

PolitiFact Oregon has issued a correction to a previous ruling regarding a statement made by the Oregon Republican Party. The party claimed that Republican candidate Rob Cornilles had the endorsements of various local mayors, including Democrats and Independents. 

Initially, PolitiFact Oregon ruled the statement as True. However, further investigation revealed that most of the mayors on the list were registered Republicans. Upon closer examination, it was discovered that six mayors were not registered Republicans, including three registered Democrats. 

One of the mayors, Amity Mayor Michael Cape, was initially reported as a registered member of the Independent Party of Oregon. However, it was found that he is actually a non-affiliated voter. The confusion arose from a change in terminology in 2007, when the Independent Party of Oregon was officially recognized by the Secretary of State. Prior to this, individuals registered as unaffiliated voters could be referred to as independent voters.

In a later interview, Mayor Cape clarified that he considers himself independent, but not a registered member of the Independent Party. The Oregon Republican Party stated that they intended to use a lower case "i" when referring to Independents, which would have been more accurate. However, the capitalization of the word "Independent" makes a difference in this context. 

As a result, PolitiFact Oregon has corrected its previous ruling from True to False.

A congressional hearing on the Trump administration's student debt policy turned contentious for Education Secretary Betsy DeVos, with Democrats criticizing her actions and Republicans defending her response to Obama-era rules.

The Obama administration finalized these changes in 2016, following the closure of Corinthian Colleges, a for-profit chain, amid allegations of fraud. DeVos subsequently sought to revise the rules, leading to extensive litigation, including a contempt of court finding against her. DeVos attributed the backlog of tens of thousands of cases to the Obama administration and announced changes, including tiers of loan relief.

During the hearing, U.S. Representative Frederica Wilson, a Democrat from South Florida and former school board member, criticized DeVos, stating that she is attempting to "destroy public education." Wilson also suggested that DeVos is the "most unpopular person in our government," citing millions of Americans who may vote to remove her in the 2020 elections.

Ranking Republican on the committee, Representative Virginia Foxx of North Carolina, deemed Wilson's comments "over the line." DeVos' confirmation in 2017 was a contentious process, requiring a tie-breaking vote by Vice President Mike Pence. DeVos, a longtime Republican donor from Michigan, is an advocate for vouchers and charter schools.

Fact-checkers examined the veracity of Wilson's statement about DeVos' popularity.
