State Senate hopeful Dan Gecker, a Democrat running for the 10th District seat, recently stated that the United States is one of a kind when it comes to healthcare. During an Aug. 18 candidates' forum, Gecker noted that among the 25 wealthiest nations, the U.S. is the only one that does not provide basic health coverage to its citizens.

Gecker's comment was in reference to universal coverage, a system in which all citizens receive national assistance in paying for healthcare costs. To verify his statement, Gecker pointed to a report from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), a group of 34 nations that aim to improve trade and economic development.

According to the OECD report, only two countries – the U.S. and Mexico – do not offer universal healthcare. A chart in the report shows that all other OECD nations provide coverage for more than 90% of their population.

However, the OECD's roster of member nations does not directly translate to a list of the 25 wealthiest countries. Gecker also directed attention to the World Bank's ranking of the wealthiest nations based on their gross domestic product (GDP) per capita. Approximately two-thirds of the nations on the World Bank's list of the 25 wealthiest countries belong to the OECD.

To further investigate, researchers compared the World Bank's ranking with a list of nations that provide universal health care. Two organizations provided relevant information: the New York State Department of Health and a 2010 study by researchers in the United Kingdom and the U.S.

Among high-GDP-per-capita nations, universal care coverage is the norm. However, only three of the 25 wealthiest nations – the U.S., Saudi Arabia, and Qatar – were not listed as having universal healthcare.

The embassy for Qatar confirmed that the country provides universal healthcare. Saudi Arabia is also listed as providing universal healthcare in a June 2012 article from The Atlantic magazine. While the Saudi Arabian embassy did not respond to repeated requests for confirmation, a 1998 study published in the Journal of Family Community Medicine indicates that Saudi Arabia's policy is to provide free, comprehensive, and universal healthcare services to all citizens.

Additionally, a 2012 op-ed by David de Ferranti, former vice president of the World Bank, and Julio Frenk, former dean of the Harvard School of Public Health, supports Gecker's statement. The authors wrote, "Except for the United States, the 25 wealthiest nations have some form of universal coverage."

Two other healthcare analysts also corroborated this finding. Andrea Feigl, a visiting scientist at Harvard and co-author of the 2010 U.K.-U.S. report, stated that the United States is still working towards universal healthcare coverage and is the last developed country to do so. The World Health Organization also noted in a September 2014 report that the United States is "currently the only high-income country without nearly universal healthcare coverage."

Our analysis concludes that Gecker's statement is supported by substantial evidence. While it is difficult to definitively say that the U.S. is the only nation without universal coverage, the available data strongly suggest that this is the case. Therefore, we rate Gecker's statement as True.

U.S. Rep. Bobby Scott Cites Data on High School Dropout Rate in Push for Legislation

U.S. Representative Bobby Scott recently announced his intention to introduce legislation aimed at reducing the high school dropout rate. In doing so, he cited a striking statistic: nearly 2,000 high schools, approximately 12 percent of all secondary schools in the United States, account for roughly half of the nation's dropouts.

To verify the accuracy of this claim, Scott's office directed our attention to a 2007 report by Robert Balfanz, co-director of the Everyone Graduates Center at Johns Hopkins University. Balfanz's report, which utilized 2006 data, identified 1,999 high schools across the nation as "low performing" and found that these schools, representing about 14 percent of the nation's regular and vocational high schools enrolling 100 or more students, reliably produced 50 percent of America's dropouts. Balfanz referred to these schools as "dropout factories."

The report also highlighted the disproportionate impact of these schools on minority students, with 81 percent of Native American, 73 percent of African American, and 66 percent of Latino dropouts coming from these institutions. In contrast, white dropouts were more evenly distributed, with 34 percent attending these schools.

While the 2007 report provides a starting point for understanding the issue, we sought to examine more recent data. In a 2010 report titled "Building a Grad Nation," Balfanz and his co-researchers re-examined the issue using U.S. Department of Education figures. The study found that the number of the country's worst-performing schools had decreased from 2,007 in 2002 to 1,746 in 2008.

The "Building a Grad Nation" study was co-sponsored by the America's Promise Alliance, a non-profit organization co-founded by retired Army General and Secretary of State Colin Powell. The alliance has proposed a "Civic Marshall Plan" to increase the number of students completing high school.

A 2011 update of the "Building a Grad Nation" study revealed that the number of dropout factories had continued to decline, falling to 1,634 in 2009. These schools, representing about 10 to 12 percent of the nation's high schools, still produce approximately half of the nation's dropouts, according to Colleen Wilber, a spokeswoman for the America's Promise Alliance.

Notably, every state has at least one "dropout factory," which Balfanz defines as a school in which at least 40 percent of freshmen fail to make it to their senior year. For high schools that only have grades 10-12, his reports examine how sophomore year enrollment compares to the senior year.

The reports do not identify the troubled schools by name, but the largest number are located in the South. Virginia, for example, had 29 of these schools in 2009, 25 in 2008, and 26 in 2002.

Scott's proposed legislation, which has been introduced in the Senate by Democrat Tom Harkin of Iowa, aims to strengthen regulations developed in 2008 that require states to use the same formula in reporting high school graduation rates. The bill also sets a national graduation rate goal of 90 percent. The national high school graduation rate was 74.9 percent in 2008, the last year for which data was available.

In conclusion, Scott's claim that nearly 2,000 high schools, about 12 percent of those in the U.S., produce half the nation's dropouts is supported by data from multiple sources, including the 2007 report and the updated "Building a Grad Nation" study. While the number of low-performing schools has decreased, the issue remains a pressing concern, and Scott's proposed legislation aims to address it.

We rate Scott's claim as True.

Wisconsin's Telecommunications Law in Need of Update

Wisconsin's telecommunications law has not been revised since the early 1990s, a time when beepers and fax machines were the norm. The industry is now regulated by laws that date back to the rotary phone era, and a recent bill aims to bring the state's laws up to speed with the modern telecommunications landscape.

The telecom deregulation bill, which was passed with bipartisan support in May 2011, seeks to remove regulations that require phone companies to invest in landline technology. Proponents of the bill argue that this change will allow companies to redirect their resources towards broadband expansion, which will lead to economic growth.

According to a study cited by state Sen. Rich Zipperer, the bill could create 50,000 jobs and result in $2.6 billion in new investment in the state. However, experts have questioned the basis of these numbers, citing a study from ConnectKentucky, a broadband expansion project that was conducted in Kentucky between 2005 and 2007.

The study found that a 7 percent increase in broadband adoption led to an estimated $1.8 billion in direct annual income growth and 50,748 jobs created or saved. However, critics have pointed out that the study was conducted in a different economic climate and that the numbers have been extrapolated to other states without considering the specific conditions in Wisconsin.

Other studies have estimated the economic impact of broadband expansion, but their projections are subject to estimation error and depend on various assumptions. A 2007 study by the Brookings Institution found that a one percentage point increase in broadband adoption is associated with nearly 300,000 more jobs, but this projection was made before the recent recession.

The Communication Workers of America has also cited a study that claims each additional $5 billion investment in broadband creates 250,000 jobs. However, this report did not provide a Wisconsin-specific number.

When asked about the estimate he has cited, Zipperer acknowledged that it's impossible to predict how many jobs will stem from deregulating landline telephone service. Wired Wisconsin executive director Thad Nation also noted that telecom companies have made "no direct promises" about how much they will expand broadband service.

Despite these uncertainties, the bill's proponents argue that deregulation will lead to economic growth and job creation. TDS Telecommunications Corp., a phone company that is shifting its emphasis to broadband, has invested $100 million in Wisconsin in the past three years and is advertising 60 job openings based on future growth. However, the use of the oft-cited 50,000 number has been questioned due to its basis in a study from another state and its ties to the telecommunications industry.

Georgia's Job Market Remains a Challenge Despite Election Promises

The issue of job creation was a central theme in the recent election season in Georgia, with politicians promising to bring "real jobs for real people" to the state. However, a prominent economist has cautioned that there are limited options for state government to stimulate the labor market in the short term.

David Wyss, chief economist for Standard & Poor's, made this point during a boot camp for state legislators in December. According to Wyss, states cannot run budget deficits, which means that any tax cuts would have to be offset by reductions in government spending, effectively neutralizing any potential stimulus.

Wyss' comments were echoed by several experts who were consulted by AJC PolitiFact Georgia. Kelly McCutchen, president of the Georgia Public Policy Foundation, agreed that the idea of state government stimulating job growth through spending is "absolutely correct." Jon Shure, deputy director of the State Fiscal Project for the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, also concurred with Wyss, noting that short-term job gains are largely driven by regional, national, and global economic factors.

While some experts, such as Brian Riedl of the Heritage Foundation, suggested that tax cuts could have a marginal impact on job creation in the short term, none argued that state government could cause an immediate, major gain. In fact, experts generally placed the state's ability to create jobs for the short term between limited and marginal.

Georgia's unemployment rate remained high in November, hovering just above 10 percent, according to the state Department of Labor. The state's economic challenges are likely to be a major focus of the 2011 legislative session, which begins on Monday. However, experts suggest that state government's options for stimulating job growth in the short term are limited, and that any efforts to do so would need to be carefully balanced with the need to balance the state budget.

Ahead of a fundraising visit to Texas by Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney, U.S. Rep. Charlie Gonzalez, a Democrat from San Antonio, criticized the former Massachusetts governor's immigration positions.

In a conference call organized by the Democratic National Committee on March 27, 2012, Gonzalez expressed concern about Romney's stance on immigration enforcement. Specifically, Gonzalez stated that while Romney was in Arizona, he believed the state's immigration-enforcement law, Senate Bill 1070, should be the template for federal immigration laws.

To verify Gonzalez's claim, the DNC pointed to Romney's response to a question during the Feb. 22, 2012, Republican presidential debate in Arizona. In the debate, Romney praised Arizona's use of the E-Verify system, which allows employers to verify the legal status of employees. He noted that the number of people in Arizona who are here illegally had dropped by 14 percent since the system was implemented, compared to a 7 percent decrease nationwide.

However, an examination of Romney's response reveals that he was actually referring to a different Arizona law, the Legal Arizona Workers Act, which requires employers to use E-Verify. This law was enacted in 2007 and is separate from the 2010 immigration-enforcement law that Gonzalez mentioned.

Dan Nowicki, a national political reporter for the Arizona Republic, questioned the interpretation of Romney's statement, pointing out that the E-Verify requirement was not part of SB 1070. Instead, Romney was describing a part of the 2007 employer-sanctions law, which requires employers to use a federal electronic system to verify the eligibility of new hires.

Romney spokesman Ryan Williams confirmed that the former governor was referring to the E-Verify requirement as the model, not SB 1070. However, Gonzalez and the DNC argued that Romney's praise for Arizona's immigration-enforcement law and his vow to drop the federal challenge to it as president suggested that he supported the law as a model for federal immigration laws.

Romney has also expressed support for the concept of "attrition through enforcement," which is the strategy behind SB 1070. This approach aims to make it difficult for illegal immigrants to live in the United States by denying them work, driver's licenses, and public benefits, and by stepping up enforcement.

In addition, Romney has touted the endorsement of Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach, who helped draft SB 1070. Kobach has served as an adviser on immigration issues to Romney's 2012 campaign and has encouraged the Romney campaign to take a stand of attrition through enforcement.

Our analysis

While Gonzalez could have targeted Romney's vow to drop the federal challenge to Arizona's immigration-enforcement law as president, his statement to reporters mischaracterizes Romney's salute to Arizona's E-Verify requirement. We rate the Texan's claim as False.

A recent online post claiming that Lance Armstrong, the former professional cyclist, has died of stage 4 colon cancer has been deemed false. The post, which allegedly announced Armstrong's death on Facebook by his daughter, Anna, has been widely debunked by Armstrong himself.

In response to an inquiry from the Austin American-Statesman, Armstrong texted, "Ha, ha, yeah, weird," indicating that the report was indeed a fabrication. Armstrong's social media accounts also contain evidence of his denial, including a May 12, 2017, video post on his Instagram account. In the video, Armstrong is seen reacting to a fake news report of his death on the fox-news24.com website, which has been identified as a fake news site attempting to mimic Fox News.

The fox-news24.com story cited Armstrong's daughter, Anna, as the source of the news, but a December 2016 Daily Mail news story about an Armstrong family Christmas card reveals that Armstrong does not have a child by that name. An Armstrong representative, Mark Higgins, has also confirmed that Armstrong is alive.

PolitiFact has previously rated the fox-news24.com site as "Pants on Fire" due to its history of disseminating false information. In this case, Armstrong's denial and the evidence of his earlier social media post have confirmed that the report of his death is entirely false.

A Recent Social Media Article Falsely Links Seasonal Flu Vaccine to Increased COVID-19 Risk

A social media article shared on April 16 has been flagged by Facebook as part of its efforts to combat false news and misinformation. The article, published on a self-described "conscious media" website, claims that a new study has found a significant association between the flu vaccine and an increased risk of contracting COVID-19.

However, the article relies on a 2019 study from the U.S. Armed Forces Health Surveillance Branch, which was published in the journal Vaccine in 2020. The study focused on Department of Defense personnel and examined the relationship between flu vaccination and the risk of contracting other respiratory viruses. The study found no connection between the flu shot and an increased risk of contracting COVID-19.

The study's data actually referred to seasonal common coronaviruses in 2017-18, not the new coronavirus that causes COVID-19. This distinction is clarified in the full article, but is ambiguous in the headline. Richard Watanabe, a preventative medicine professor at USC, notes that the article does not provide strong support for its claims, as the study found little correlation between the flu vaccine and respiratory viruses.

In fact, the U.S. Armed Forces study concluded that further research is needed, as the overall results showed little to no evidence supporting the association of virus interference and influenza vaccination. The study found that vaccinated individuals were more likely to have no pathogen detected and reduced risk of influenza compared to unvaccinated individuals.

The article also fails to mention parts of the study that question the data linking coronavirus cases to the influenza vaccine. For instance, the U.S. Armed Forces study referenced a 2013 study with similar results, which found no association between influenza vaccination and various respiratory viruses, including coronaviruses.

Edward Belongia, an infectious disease epidemiologist who worked on the 2013 study, explained that there is little scientific data to support the speculative theory of the flu vaccine increasing the risk of other respiratory viruses. While the article does specify that the U.S. Armed Forces study was testing common coronaviruses and not COVID-19, the headline is ambiguous and misleading.

A recent interactive feature on Sen. John McCain's campaign website has drawn attention from political enthusiasts, allowing visitors to guess how much the Democrats' budget resolution would raise America's tax bill. The feature, described as a poll, presents four options, including zero, $500 million, $200 billion, and $500 billion.

McCain's campaign is using this tool to emphasize his fiscal conservative credentials and portray the Democratic Party as reckless spenders. The website asks visitors to sign an online petition in support of "restoring fiscal sanity," which requires them to provide their names, email addresses, and zip codes.

However, budget experts have pointed out that the poll is misleading. Budget resolutions, which serve as blueprints for future spending, do not have the force of law. They are used by the majority party to make a political statement and set nonbinding parameters for considering tax and spending legislation. As a result, it is technically incorrect to say that the budget resolution will raise, lower, or keep taxes the same.

The $500 billion figure cited by McCain's campaign is also misleading, as the fiscal 2009 budget resolutions adopted by the House and Senate in March do not include line items on tax proposals. Instead, the Democrats who wrote the resolutions assume that many of President Bush's 2001 and 2003 tax cuts will expire at the end of 2010, which would bring more revenue into the government's coffers.

When asked about the origin of the $500 billion figure, the McCain campaign did not respond. However, it is the same amount that other Republicans have used, noting that it is the difference between revenue calculations done with the tax cuts expiring and with the tax cuts being extended. The Congressional Budget Office, a nonpartisan arm of Congress, has conducted five-year revenue projections that assume all of the Bush tax cuts are allowed to expire, and these estimates are close to what the budget resolutions project for the same time frame.

Republicans have used this figure as evidence that Democrats want to eliminate all of the Bush tax cuts. However, other facts need to be taken into account. Democratic lawmakers who wrote the budget resolution also support extending at least some of the tax cuts that have helped lower- and middle-income taxpayers. In fact, during the full Senate debate on the chamber's resolution, lawmakers adopted an amendment by Senate Finance Committee Chairman Max Baucus, D-Mont., that would extend the child tax credit, marriage-penalty relief provisions, and other components in the 2001 tax package.

Democrats maintain that they have not yet made final decisions on which tax cuts will stay and which will go, and that those tax cuts that are extended will be offset by tax increases elsewhere or by spending cuts. The budget resolution does not provide enough specifics to know the net effect on taxes, up or down.

In conclusion, while budget resolutions do not have the force of law and do not contain enough specific language for anyone to calculate a particular tax increase, the McCain campaign's claim that the budget resolution would raise taxes by $500 billion is inaccurate.

A recent attack ad against Sen. Ted Cruz, sponsored by the New Day for America super PAC, has been criticized for its misleading content. The ad, which targets Cruz's association with Ohio Gov. John Kasich, accuses Cruz of lying and features a growing nose, a reference to the "Pinocchio" effect.

The ad in question was actually a response to a previous commercial released by the Trusted Leadership super PAC, which supports Cruz. The original ad claimed that Kasich had received hundreds of thousands of dollars from liberal billionaire George Soros, a claim that was later debunked by PolitiFact Ohio as False. The Soros-Kasich connection was based on a donor who managed assets for Soros from 1988 to 2000 and another who started his own hedge fund with seed money from Soros.

New Day for America complained to Wisconsin television stations that aired the Trusted Leadership ad, arguing that they were not obligated to run false or misleading super PAC ads. At least four stations reportedly pulled the ad after receiving the complaint. However, the Trusted Leadership super PAC subsequently revised the ad, replacing the reference to Soros with "cronies."

A closer examination of the New Day ad reveals a larger issue with its claim that Cruz is a liar. The ad specifically targets Cruz, despite the fact that the deceptive ad was released by his super PAC, Trusted Leadership. Under federal law, super PACs are not allowed to coordinate with the candidate or their campaign. While this separation is intended to prevent coordination, it is not always clear-cut, and campaigns can easily be aware of their super PAC's activities.

The New Day ad's use of the "Pinocchio" effect to imply that Cruz is a liar is itself misleading, given that the ad is actually targeting Cruz's super PAC. This irony is noteworthy, and the claim made in the New Day ad is rated False.

**Georgia's Roadway Death Toll Rises: Is Driver Behavior to Blame?**

The heartbreaking news of five Georgia Southern nursing students who lost their lives in a devastating pileup crash outside Savannah last week serves as a stark reminder that the roads can be treacherous, even for those who are not doing anything wrong. The senseless tragedy is a sobering reality check for drivers across the state, where the number of traffic fatalities is skyrocketing.

As the Georgia Department of Transportation (DOT) desperately tries to grab the attention of drivers, the numbers are nothing short of chilling. "GEORGIA ROADWAY FATALITIES THIS YEAR: 388," flashed a DOT sign on I-75 in Cobb County on Thursday. "STAY ALERT. STAY ALIVE." But the question remains: is it too late?

With over three deaths occurring every day, the state is averaging 100 fatalities a month on its roadways, putting it on track for a staggering 1,200 fatalities by year's end. This would mark a 4.6 percent increase from 2014 numbers, and the first year-to-year increase in nine years. The statistics are nothing short of alarming.

Terri Pope, spokeswoman for the Northeast DOT region, painted a dire picture when asked about the signs and numbers behind them. "Only 38 percent of drivers were wearing seat belts, and 69 percent failed to maintain their lane – behaviors that experts say save lives behind the wheel." The data is clear: driver error is a major factor in these crashes.

But what's even more disturbing is the rise in distracted driving. According to the Governor's Office of Highway Safety, the number of fatal crashes in which distracted driving was a factor jumped nearly 64 percent in five years. The increase in the number of deaths was even worse: up nearly 73 percent in the same period. The numbers are a stark warning sign that drivers are putting their lives at risk by driving distracted.

As the summer driving season approaches, transportation officials are left with a daunting task: getting the message through to drivers that their behavior is putting lives at risk. The state DOT has begun flashing messages on Georgia roadways, but will it be enough to prevent more tragedies? Only time will tell.

A recent Facebook post claims that there are 5,615 projected coal-powered plants in just eight countries, with the United States having 15 plants and no new ones under construction. However, an investigation by our team found that the post's numbers are inaccurate.

Breaking down the numbers by country, the tracker shows that China has 1,032 operational coal plants, 126 under construction, and 76 planned for construction, totaling 1,234 plants. In contrast, the United States has 296 operational coal plants, but none under construction.

Experts agree that the growth of coal is not happening in the United States, but rather in developing countries such as China, India, and Southeast Asia. This is due to the fact that coal is cheaper, widely available, and easier to store and transport in these regions.

Anna Mikulska, a fellow for the Center for Energy Studies at Rice University, notes that the developing world is more likely to rely on coal due to its affordability and accessibility. In contrast, the United States and Europe are turning away from coal due to the abundance of cheap and clean-burning natural gas.

The Global Coal Plant Tracker is a comprehensive database of coal-fired power stations, maintained by the Global Energy Monitor, a non-profit organization with board members from environmental groups such as Clean Energy Action and Greenpeace. The tracker's data is widely regarded as a reliable source of information on coal plant numbers and capacity.

In conclusion, the Facebook post's claim of 5,615 projected coal-powered plants is an exaggeration and not supported by evidence. The actual number of coal plants, according to the Global Coal Plant Tracker, is significantly lower at 3,074.

Georgia's New Milestones Tests Yield Low Scores, Reflecting Concerns About Previous CRCT Assessments

The state's first round of Georgia Milestones tests, administered on September 3, has revealed low scores among students. According to the results, only 10 percent of students who took a language arts or science course at any grade level finished in the top category of distinguished learners. In math, 60 percent of all Georgia students scored as beginning or developing learners.

State School Superintendent Richard Woods attributes the low scores to the new test's higher standards, which are more comparable to national benchmarks and essential for students to be college- and career-ready. However, some have raised questions about the accuracy of Woods' claim that the previous Criterion-Referenced Competency Tests (CRCT) set some of the lowest expectations for student proficiency in the nation.

The CRCT was a primary measure of student achievement in Georgia from 2000 to 2014 and was used to determine whether schools made adequate yearly progress under the federal No Child Left Behind law. The test was also used to determine promotion to the next grade for students in certain subjects.

Critics of the CRCT have long argued that the test was too easy, pointing to the wide disparity between passing rates on the CRCT and the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), considered the gold standard of tests. For example, in 2006, The Education Trust reported that 87 percent of Georgia fourth-graders were considered "proficient" in reading on the CRCT, but only 26 percent of a sampling of those same students were proficient on the 2005 NAEP reading test.

Subsequent reports from The Education Trust and the Governor's Office of Student Achievement have also highlighted the low bar set by the CRCT for student proficiency. A 2013 report from the Governor's Office of Student Achievement found that Georgia had the lowest mathematics and reading cut scores in the nation, with students needing to answer fewer test questions correctly to pass the test.

A NAEP Mapping Study also found that Georgia had the lowest numeric 4th grade reading expectations in the nation and ranked third from the bottom on 4th grade math expectations. The study used NAEP as a common scale to compare one state's expectations of what their students should know and be able to do in order to be considered "proficient" on their state assessments to other states.

State Superintendent Woods has acknowledged that the CRCT set a low bar for student proficiency, stating that "too many students were labeled as proficient when, in reality, they had not fully mastered the standards and needed additional support." He also noted that this has hurt students who need to be competitive with others across the country and has made it difficult for teachers to have a true picture of their students' academic strengths and weaknesses.

In light of the evidence, we rate State Superintendent Richard Woods' statement that the CRCT set some of the lowest expectations for student proficiency in the nation as True.

Richard Ojeda, a Democrat from West Virginia who is considering a presidential run in 2020, recently released a video clip criticizing General Motors' decision to close five plants and lay off over 14,000 employees in late November. The video, shared on Twitter on November 27, 2018, called out the company's announcement and highlighted what Ojeda perceived as a lack of gratitude towards its workers.

In the tweet, Ojeda stated, "I'm in Detroit at General Motors HQ. We bailed you out. We gave you tax breaks. Your workers are the reason your CEO took home almost 22 MILLION DOLLARS last year alone (295x your company's average employee). And this is how you repay them? #CorporateGreed."

PolitiFact investigated whether Ojeda's claim that General Motors' CEO, Mary Barra, earned almost $22 million last year, a sum that was 295 times the company's average employee, was accurate. According to Stephanie Rice, General Motors' assistant manager of finance communications, Barra's total compensation package for the year was $21.96 million, which was approximately 295 times the median employee salary.

These figures are publicly reported to the Securities and Exchange Commission and have garnered media attention. Notably, Barra's compensation package for 2018 was lower than her 2016 compensation of $22.58 million.

While the 295-to-1 ratio between Barra's compensation and the median employee salary may seem significant, it is not an isolated case. Research by the Economic Policy Institute, a labor-aligned think tank, found that the 2017 CEO-to-worker compensation ratio among 350 large U.S. companies was 312-to-1. This ratio has increased significantly over the years, with the highest ratio recorded in 2000 at 344-to-1.

The Economic Policy Institute also noted that the current ratio is far greater than the 20-to-1 ratio in 1965 and more than five times greater than the 58-to-1 ratio in 1989.

It's worth noting that Ojeda used the term "average" employee, which may lead some readers to assume it refers to the mean salary. However, the SEC data uses the median salary, which is a type of average but is not commonly referred to as such.

PolitiFact contacted Ojeda for comment but did not receive a response.

Our ruling
Ojeda stated that General Motors' CEO, Mary Barra, "took home almost 22 MILLION DOLLARS last year alone (295x your company's average employee)." The company confirmed both figures, which are required by law to be reported to the government. We rate the statement True.

He further stated that if the Border Patrol apprehends eight or nine thousand people a week, that is more than the number of people born in Texas each week.

According to Patrick's campaign spokesman, Alejandro Garcia, the senator picked up on the comparison from a briefing by state officials during a visit to the Rio Grande Valley in June 2014. Garcia stated that the comparison illustrates the seriousness of border apprehensions.

In 2010, 385,746 babies were born in Texas.

However, the data also revealed that the births occurred three years before the apprehensions, making an apples-to-apples comparison challenging. PolitiFact obtained up-to-date data on apprehensions and births, which enabled a comparison of the two by month for all of 2013 and the first six months of 2014. The data showed that apprehensions outnumbered births in 11 of the 18 months, including the latest months, February through June 2014.

To gauge Patrick's claim over the latest full year of data available when he spoke, PolitiFact looked at totals covering July 2013 through June 2014. In those months, there were about 393,299 births in Texas, while the Border Patrol tallied 480,404 apprehensions. Monthly apprehensions fluctuated significantly, ranging from a low of 28,671 in January 2014 to a high of 60,689 in May 2014.

In fiscal 2011, 380,481 children were born in Texas, and the Border Patrol apprehended 327,577.

PolitiFact's analysis concluded that Patrick's claim was accurate when he spoke, as apprehensions had sufficiently outnumbered births in the five months preceding his radio interview. However, this claim may not hold if apprehensions decrease sufficiently. Based on the data, PolitiFact rates Patrick's claim as True.

U.S. Rep. Lamar Smith, R-San Antonio, recently expressed concerns about the Development, Relief and Education for Alien Minors Act, also known as the DREAM Act. In an op-ed published in The Hill on November 30, Smith argued that the bill, which aims to provide a pathway to citizenship for undocumented residents brought to the United States as minors, would have negative consequences for the American people.

One of Smith's primary concerns is that individuals who become citizens under the DREAM Act could sponsor their undocumented parents for legalization. According to Smith, this would allow individuals to sponsor their parents for legalization once they turn 21 and become citizens.

The U.S. House of Representatives recently passed the DREAM Act with a vote of 216-198. However, the measure did not advance in the Senate, falling short of the 60 votes needed to cut off debate and bring the legislation to the floor.

A previous statement by Rep. Ted Poe, R-Humble, regarding the DREAM Act sparked a discussion about the bill's provisions. Poe claimed that individuals who become citizens under the act could sponsor their extended family members to come to the United States. However, this statement was inaccurate, as U.S. citizens are not eligible to sponsor grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins, or in-laws for legal entry into the country.

Smith's statement, on the other hand, accurately reflects the provisions of federal law, which permit U.S. citizens to sponsor immediate family members, including spouses, unmarried children, and adopted children under 21, for an "immediate relative immigrant visa." Additionally, citizens 21 and older can sponsor their parents for legal permanent residence.

However, there is a key distinction that Smith's statement does not address. According to Michelle Mittelstadt, a spokeswoman for the Washington-based Migration Policy Institute, it is highly unlikely that individuals who become citizens under the DREAM Act would be eligible to sponsor their parents for legalization by the age of 21. This is because individuals who become citizens under the act must first spend 10 years in non-immigrant status and then three years as a legal permanent resident before they can apply for citizenship.

The DREAM Act has undergone various iterations, but recent legislation requires that undocumented residents be younger than 30, have been brought to the United States at age 15 or younger, and have lived in the country for at least five years prior to the measure becoming law to be eligible for the act's benefits. To become a citizen under the act, an individual must meet several requirements, including completing two years of higher education or serving in the military, being of "good moral character," and spending a total of 13 years in the United States in various immigration statuses.

While Smith's statement is accurate in its description of the sponsorship process for immediate family members, it is misleading in its suggestion that individuals who become citizens under the DREAM Act would be eligible to sponsor their parents for legalization by the age of 21. For this reason, we rate Smith's statement as Mostly True.

California Gubernatorial Candidate Antonio Villaraigosa Weighs in on Immigration Reform

During a recent MSNBC interview, Antonio Villaraigosa, a Democratic candidate for California governor, addressed the contentious issue of immigration reform. In response to President Trump's speech on combating MS-13 gang members, Villaraigosa expressed skepticism about the effectiveness of deporting undocumented immigrants as a crime-reduction strategy.

Villaraigosa's comments were based on a 2015 study by the National Academy of Sciences, which found that immigrants are significantly less likely to commit crimes than native-born individuals. The study noted that the presence of large numbers of immigrants appears to lower crime rates. This finding has been supported by subsequent research, including a March 2017 study by the libertarian Cato Institute, which found that both legal and undocumented immigrants are underrepresented in the incarcerated population compared to native-born individuals.

To examine Villaraigosa's claim, PolitiFact conducted a fact-check, relying on research from various sources, including the American Immigration Council and the Public Policy Institute of California. The analysis revealed that immigrants are indeed less likely to commit crimes than native-born individuals, with incarceration rates significantly lower among foreign-born men compared to their native-born counterparts.

PolitiFact also noted that as the immigrant population has increased, crime rates have decreased. Between 1990 and 2013, the foreign-born share of the U.S. population increased, and the number of unauthorized immigrants rose, while the violent crime rate decreased by 48 percent and the property crime rate fell by 41 percent.

However, some researchers have cautioned that the relationship between immigration and crime is complex and requires further study. The Center for Immigration Studies has argued that the lack of data and contradictory information has led to a "confused" understanding of the issue.

In light of this evidence, PolitiFact California has ruled Villaraigosa's claim that "undocumented immigrants commit less crimes than the native born" as Mostly True. While the statement is accurate, it requires clarification or additional information to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the issue.

PolitiFact California's fact-checking series, Tracking The Truth, aims to provide a thorough examination of claims made by candidates in the 2018 California governor's race.

Rhode Island Health Department and Union Settle Dispute Over Flu Vaccination Mandate

The Rhode Island Department of Health and the SEIU Healthcare Employees Union, District 1199, have reached a settlement in a court dispute over state regulations requiring healthcare workers to receive flu immunizations.

The regulations, which were implemented to reduce the spread of flu to patients, required healthcare workers to either receive the vaccination or wear surgical masks when interacting with patients. The union had filed a lawsuit in December, arguing that the regulations violated due-process and collective-bargaining rights.

The union withdrew its lawsuit as the flu season was winding down, stating that it hoped to reach a compromise with the health department. A review of the union's complaint revealed a claim that there is no clinical evidence that vaccinating healthcare workers protects patients.

A review of national health agencies, including the CDC and the American Medical Association, found that these organizations strongly recommend that all healthcare employees receive the flu vaccination. The CDC reported that 66.9% of healthcare workers were vaccinated for the 2011-12 flu season.

Several peer-reviewed studies have investigated the effectiveness of vaccinating healthcare workers in reducing flu transmission to patients. One study published in The Lancet in 2000 found that vaccinations of healthcare workers were associated with a substantial decrease in deaths among patients. Another study published in BMJ in 2004 found decreases in deaths and influenza-like illness among nursing home residents when more workers were vaccinated.

A study published in the journal Vaccine in 2009 used computer modeling to simulate a flu outbreak and found that healthcare employee vaccinations reduce flu transmission.

The union was contacted to request data supporting its position, and a representative stated that while vaccinating healthcare workers may seem like a "no-brainer" for preventing flu transmission, there is no clinically proven connection between vaccination and reduced transmission. The representative cited three systematic reviews that concluded there is no clinically proven connection.

However, a review published in 2010 by the Cochrane Collaboration found that vaccinating healthcare workers who care for the elderly did not show any effect on laboratory-proven influenza, pneumonia, or deaths from pneumonia among patients. However, the review did find that vaccinations had an effect on influenza-like illnesses, hospital admissions, and overall mortality of the elderly.

The debate over the effectiveness of flu vaccines is ongoing, with some studies suggesting that the current vaccines may not be effective enough. Our review of the evidence found that while there are disputes over the conclusions drawn from the studies, there is indeed evidence that vaccinating healthcare workers can reduce flu transmission to patients.

Therefore, we rate the union's claim that "there is no clinical evidence that vaccinating healthcare workers protects patients" as False.

Georgia Republican U.S. Rep. Paul Broun has announced his candidacy for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by fellow Republican Saxby Chambliss. Since declaring his intention to run, Broun has emphasized his willingness to work with lawmakers from both sides of the aisle to address the country's most pressing issues. This approach marks a departure from his typical style, which has often been characterized by a more confrontational tone and criticism of President Barack Obama.

A recent fundraiser letter, however, reveals a different side of Broun. In the letter, he expresses strong conservative views and criticizes Democratic leaders for allegedly overstepping their constitutional authority. Broun also aligns himself with prominent conservative figures, including former Florida congressman Allen West and U.S. Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky. He notes that, excluding foreign policy, his voting record is virtually identical to that of Ron Paul, the father of Rand Paul and a former Texas congressman.

Broun's alignment with Ron Paul is not unusual, as politicians often seek to associate themselves with popular figures within their party. PolitiFact Georgia examined Broun's claim about his voting record and similarity to Ron Paul's.

Both Broun and Ron Paul have consistently advocated for limited government and reduced spending. Additionally, they share a medical background, with Ron Paul serving as a military flight surgeon and obstetrician-gynecologist, and Broun practicing general medicine and operating a house-call-based business.

PolitiFact Georgia analyzed 383 votes cast by Broun and Ron Paul during their concurrent time in office, which began in July 2007. The review revealed that the two men voted differently on the same bill 42 times, or about 11 percent of the total votes. However, if votes related to defense topics are excluded as foreign policy, the number of opposing votes drops to 23, or about 6 percent of the total votes.

When asked for comment on the letter, Broun's staff did not respond.

Kennesaw State University professor Kerwin Swint noted that Ron Paul's image as a conservative is well-established, which may explain why Broun and he agree on many issues, except foreign policy. Swint added that, on foreign policy, Ron Paul tends to hold more liberal views than Obama.

Last week, TheTeaParty.net, a conservative grassroots organization, endorsed Broun in the U.S. Senate race. The group's founder, Todd Cefaratti, praised Broun's campaign, saying it will be supported by thousands of citizens concerned about the country's future.

PolitiFact Georgia found that Broun's statement about his voting record and Ron Paul's being virtually identical, except for foreign policy, is accurate. The two men's congressional terms overlapped from 2007 to January 2013, during which time their votes differed just 6 percent of the time after excluding foreign policy-related votes.

PolitiFact rated Broun's statement True.

Staff writer Karishma Mehrotra contributed to this article.

NARAL Pro-Choice Virginia recently released a video criticizing Republican Governor Bob McDonnell's stance on funding for sex education programs. The video features a montage of numbers that aim to highlight the costs and consequences of McDonnell's policies.

The claims made in the video include an approximate cost of $400,000 to Virginians for funding ineffective abstinence-only-until-marriage programs, as well as a loss of $2.5 million in federal funding for comprehensive sex education programs due to McDonnell's political agenda.

To verify the accuracy of NARAL's claims, we reached out to Tarina Keene, the executive director of NARAL Pro-Choice Virginia, for sources of the information.

Regarding the statement that abstinence-only education costs the state $400,000, Keene explained that this figure refers to the state's match money for a federal grant for abstinence-only sex education. The grant, administered by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, aims to promote abstinence until marriage to prevent teen pregnancy and sexually-transmitted diseases.

In September 2010, HHS announced that Virginia would receive an $889,973 grant for abstinence education for fiscal 2010. States have until September 30, 2012, to spend the money, with the federal government covering 57 percent of the cost. Participating states are required to provide the remaining 43 percent of the cost, which can come from various sources, including state coffers, foundation dollars, and in-kind donations.

According to Jeff Caldwell, a spokesman for the governor, the state is paying $382,688 towards the match, with the remaining amount coming from in-kind contributions and community organizations awarded contracts to implement the sexual abstinence programs. This figure is close to NARAL's estimate of $400,000.

Caldwell noted that the state has received federal abstinence education funding under previous governors dating back to the 1990s. However, in 2007, Democratic Governor Tim Kaine cut the state's funding for abstinence-only education, which was reversed by McDonnell last year.

McDonnell also chose not to seek funding for the Personal Responsibility Education Program, which teaches students about contraception in addition to abstinence. Unlike the federal abstinence-only money, the comprehensive sex education grant requires no match. McDonnell's decision not to participate drew criticism from NARAL and Planned Parenthood Advocates of Virginia.

Regarding the second part of NARAL's claim, that Virginia lost $2.5 million in federal money for comprehensive sex education under McDonnell, the organization cited an HHS 49-page announcement of the PREP grant, which was created under the 2010 health care reform law.

The HHS synopsis shows that Virginia was estimated to receive a total of $2,593,487 during fiscal years 2010 and 2011. This figure is close to NARAL's estimate of $2.5 million.

However, NARAL is understating its case. States that did not apply for the grant in fiscal 2010 and 2011 are not eligible to seek funding for the 2012-2014 fiscal years. According to Kenneth Wolfe, an HHS spokesman, estimates for 2012-2014 allotments are not available.

In conclusion, NARAL's video claims that abstinence-only programs pursued under McDonnell have cost the state about $400,000, while the group says the state missed out on about $2.5 million in federal funding for comprehensive sex education. While NARAL's statement is not entirely accurate, it is true that the state spent about $400,000 for a federal abstinence-only grant and did not apply for a comprehensive sex education grant that would have sent almost $2.6 million to Virginia during fiscal year 2010 and 2011. Because Virginia is now ineligible to apply for the comprehensive grant through 2014, the state will wind up declining a much greater amount of money than NARAL claimed.

**The Dark Reality Behind Missouri's "Domestic Union" Bill**

Imagine a world where your love and commitment to your partner are reduced to nothing more than a contract. A world where the government strips away the rights and protections that come with marriage, leaving you vulnerable and exposed. That's exactly what Missouri's HB2173 bill would have done, had it not been mercifully defeated in the House Rules Committee.

The bill's sponsor, Rep. Adam Schnelting, claims he just wants the government out of the marriage business. But what he's really doing is trying to sidestep the 2015 Supreme Court decision that made same-sex marriage the law of the land. By replacing marriage licenses with "contracts of domestic union," Schnelting is attempting to erase the very concept of marriage and replace it with a hollow shell of a contract.

But what about the federal benefits that come with marriage? Don't they matter? Schnelting says that domestic unions are the legal equivalent of marriage, but the truth is far more sinister. Without a federal definition, domestic unions are nothing more than a vague term with no real meaning. And when it comes to federal benefits, they're as good as worthless.

Take Social Security, for example. The Social Security Administration recognizes some civil unions and domestic partnerships, but only in certain states. And as for immigration purposes, the Department of State doesn't even consider individuals in domestic partnerships or civil unions as spouses. It's a nightmare scenario, where your love and commitment are reduced to nothing more than a mere contract, with no real rights or protections to speak of.

And what about state benefits? Missouri's HB2173 bill would have left you with nothing but a hollow promise of equality. Without a federal definition, there's no guarantee that domestic unions would be recognized in other states, or that the dissolution of the union would be recognized as such. It's a ticking time bomb, waiting to unleash a wave of uncertainty and heartbreak on countless couples.

So, what's the truth behind Schnelting's claim that replacing marriage licenses with domestic union contracts "does not alter state or federal benefits"? The answer is simple: it's a lie. A Mostly False claim, to be exact. The reality is far more complicated, and far more devastating.

Rep. Louise Slaughter, D-Fairport, has expressed concerns that ending an Obama-era immigration policy that protects children of undocumented immigrants from deportation would have negative economic consequences.

The Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, which was rescinded by President Trump earlier this month, provides temporary relief from deportation to nearly 800,000 individuals, including over 41,000 in New York state, the fourth-highest number of any state.

Slaughter claimed in a tweet that ending DACA would harm the economy, stating, "President Trump's decision will harm our economy and endanger the future of thousands of Americans." A recent report by the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning policy research organization, estimated that the U.S. would lose $460.3 billion over a decade if working DACA recipients were deported, with New York state losing $2.6 billion annually.

The Center for American Progress based its estimate on a 2016 report by two economics professors at Queens College, which predicted that the U.S. would lose $4.7 trillion in gross domestic product by 2026 if all 11 million undocumented immigrants in the country were deported. Analysts from the Center for American Progress narrowed this finding to focus on immigrants in the labor force protected under DACA.

Other research, conducted by the Cato Institute, a libertarian public policy group, estimated that the national economy would lose $283 billion over the next decade if all DACA recipients were deported, with New York alone losing more than $49.4 billion in that time. While the two estimates differ in magnitude, they both suggest that ending DACA would have a negative impact on the economy.

DACA recipients, who are largely employed, contribute to the economy through their labor and tax payments. According to research from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, undocumented immigrants eligible for DACA contribute more than $2 billion in state and local taxes each year, with over $140 million coming from DACA-eligible immigrants in New York state.

The economic benefits of DACA are attributed to the increased labor supply, which allows businesses to expand and hire more workers. However, it's worth noting that DACA recipients are not eligible for most public benefits, such as Medicaid or food stamps.

Our analysis suggests that the available evidence supports the claim that ending DACA would have negative economic consequences. While the estimates vary in magnitude, they all indicate that deporting DACA recipients would harm the economy.

Austin Appointee's Claim on Arabic Language Misrepresents City's Linguistic Diversity

Maram Museitif, a Central Health Board of Managers member appointed by the Austin City Council, made a statement in May 2017 that Arabic is the third most-common language in Austin. However, a review of federal surveys and data from Central Health reveals that Chinese is actually the third most-prevalent language spoken in the city.

According to a press release announcing Museitif's appointment, she stated that she brings a broader representation to the board and can serve as a voice for the growing Muslim, Arab, and refugee community in Austin. Museitif also claimed to speak fluent Arabic, which she stated is the third most-common language in Austin.

However, Central Health's spokesman, Ted Burton, clarified that Museitif's statement referred specifically to the patient population served by CommUnityCare, a network of health care providers overseen by Central Health. According to patient-submitted responses, Arabic was the third most-common language spoken by patients in fiscal year 2015, with 1.1% of patients reporting speaking Arabic.

In contrast, federal surveys indicate that Chinese is the third most-prevalent language spoken in Austin, behind English and Spanish. The 2015 American Community Survey conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau found that Chinese was the third most-common spoken language in Austin, while Arabic was ranked 12th.

Ryan Robinson, the City of Austin demographer, provided a chart showing Arabic as the 10th most-prevalent language spoken in Austin, behind English, Spanish, Chinese, Vietnamese, other Asian languages, Korean, Hindi, French, and other Indic languages.

PolitiFact has rated Museitif's statement as False, as it misrepresents the linguistic diversity of Austin. While Arabic is indeed a significant language spoken by patients at Central Health clinics, it is not the third most-common language spoken in the city as a whole.

* Central Health's patient-submitted responses, fiscal year 2015
* 2015 American Community Survey, U.S. Census Bureau

U.S. Senate Candidate Tommy Thompson's Lobbying Label Debated on Campaign Trail

In the midst of the U.S. Senate campaign, Republican candidate Tommy Thompson has been referred to by his rival, Eric Hovde, and Democrats as a "corporate lobbyist." However, Thompson disputes this label, stating it is "flat out false."

Thompson's lucrative private-sector affiliation with numerous health and other companies has raised questions about his role as a consultant and advisor. As Secretary of Health and Human Services during the George W. Bush administration, Thompson oversaw industry regulators, some of whom have business dealings with the companies he advises.

According to a 2012 report by the Journal Sentinel, Thompson's net worth has reached approximately $13 million, largely accumulated in the seven years since he left government and began his career as a corporate consultant and advisor.

Hovde has pressed the claim that Thompson is a lobbyist, citing several points of evidence. These include Thompson's employment at Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld in Washington, D.C., a media report on Thompson contacting a North Carolina lawmaker, and a campaign-donation report listing Thompson's occupation as "lobbyist."

Akin Gump is a well-known lobbying firm, but it is also an international law firm. Thompson, an attorney, was listed as a partner before leaving the firm in January 2012 to campaign for U.S. Senate. While some Akin Gump partners are registered lobbyists, Thompson is not.

Federal law requires individuals to register as lobbyists if they have more than one lobbying contact in a three-month period while representing a client. The work must make up at least 20 percent of the lobbyist's work for a client. However, Thompson could limit such contacts and still avoid registration.

"We have at least 3,000 unregistered lobbyists, and the number is probably far higher than that," said Howard Marlowe, a lobbying firm president and head of the American League of Lobbyists.

Hovde's evidence, however, does not prove that Thompson is a lobbyist. The North Carolina example, in which Thompson contacted a state lawmaker about a bill, is also murky. Thompson claims he made the call on behalf of a "friend of a friend" and not as a paid consultant.

A campaign report from 2010, listing Thompson as a "lobbyist" on a donation from U.S. Sen. John Hoeven (R-North Dakota), is also disputed. Thompson's campaign suggests that Hoeven's campaign erroneously wrote in that occupation.

Thompson's affiliation with Constella Group, a North Carolina medical research firm, has also raised questions. As chairman of the firm's advisory board, Thompson was brought on to "connect" the company with U.S. and foreign governments and advise it on growth strategies. However, Thompson claims that nothing he did for Constella constituted lobbying.

In Washington, the kind of work Thompson does is often described as either a "strategic advice" consultant or a "rainmaker" whose influence and connections bring work to his firm. Bill Broydrick, a veteran lobbyist in Wisconsin and Washington, stated that a consultant's responsibility is to give their client professional advice, which is not lobbying.

Thompson's situation is reminiscent of the debate during the GOP presidential primary over Newt Gingrich's statement that he "never lobbied under any circumstance" for Freddie Mac. Gingrich acknowledged that Freddie Mac hired his consulting group but said it was only for strategic advice and broadening contacts among conservatives, not lobbying.

In rating Gingrich's claim Half True, PolitiFact National said he was technically correct but took pains to avoid being subject to the lobbying rules and use his influence as an adviser.

Thompson appears to have taken similar pains. He told us Akin Gump wanted him to register as a lobbyist, but he refused. However, when asked directly if he has ever contacted a legislator on behalf of any corporate client to urge action on a bill, Thompson was evasive, saying he couldn't say for sure.

In conclusion, Hovde's claims that Thompson was a corporate lobbyist and lobbied during the current campaign are not entirely supported by evidence. While Thompson is not a registered lobbyist, he has sold his influence and connections to firms to whom it would benefit on Capitol Hill, but did so in a way to avoid registration. Therefore, we rate this claim Half True.

California's COVID-19 Death Toll: Is Herd Immunity the Answer?

A recent Facebook post has sparked debate about the reasons behind California's relatively low number of COVID-19 deaths compared to New York. The post suggests that the state may have achieved "herd immunity," a phenomenon in which a sufficient percentage of the population is immune to a virus, thereby preventing its spread.

According to the post, researchers at Stanford's School of Medicine are conducting a study to determine whether California has indeed achieved herd immunity. The post also cites the state's status as a popular tourist destination for people from China, suggesting that the virus may have been circulating in California since October or November.

However, experts say that there is no evidence to support the claim that herd immunity is responsible for California's lower death toll. Herd immunity occurs when a sufficient percentage of the population is immune to a virus, making it unlikely to spread. However, with relatively little COVID-19 testing having been done, it is not possible to determine the level of immunity in either California or New York.

The Stanford study, which tested for coronavirus antibodies among 3,300 people in Santa Clara County, found that the infection was much more widespread than indicated by the number of confirmed cases. However, the study's findings do not provide evidence of herd immunity.

Experts from various institutions, including Boston University, Northwestern University, and Columbia University, have stated that there is no evidence of herd immunity for COVID-19. They point out that the lack of testing data makes it impossible to determine who is protected from the virus.

Another possible explanation for California's lower death toll is that the state adopted stay-at-home orders and other responses before New York did. News reports have suggested that this may have contributed to the difference in death tolls between the two states.

In conclusion, while herd immunity is a real phenomenon, there is no evidence to support the claim that it is responsible for California's lower COVID-19 death toll. Experts say that more testing is needed to determine the level of immunity in the population, and that other factors, such as the timing of stay-at-home orders, may be more significant contributors to the difference in death tolls between California and New York.

PolitiFact Ohio Analyzes Claim on Obama's Regulation Record

In a recent conference call with Ohio reporters, U.S. Sen. Rob Portman (R-Ohio) discussed a bill he co-introduced to require cost-benefit analysis and enhance business flexibility before new federal regulations and rules are issued. Portman stated that President Barack Obama's administration has imposed more regulations without a thorough assessment of their impact on businesses and jobs.

Portman claimed that the Obama administration has issued "more of these major rules" than the Clinton administration or the Bush administration during comparable times. To examine this claim, PolitiFact Ohio analyzed data from various sources, including the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and the Government Accountability Office.

According to OMB data, a "major" rule is defined as any regulation with an economic impact of at least $100 million. PolitiFact Ohio reviewed three analyses of major or economically significant rules, all using OMB data and broken down by year and presidency. The analyses were provided by Portman's Senate staff, the Regulatory Studies Center at George Washington University, and the Center for Effective Government.

The data showed that during the first three years of their tenures, Obama had 162 major rules, compared to 115 for Bush and 135 for Clinton. A similar analysis by the Regulatory Studies Center had a similar conclusion, with Obama having 217 economically significant rules in his first four years, compared to 190 for Bush in his second term.

The Center for Effective Government also analyzed new regulations since 1992 and found that Obama's record for the first 42 months of his presidency was 38 percent higher than the comparable period of Bush's first term and 36 percent higher than the comparable period in Clinton's.

While some critics have noted that the $100 million threshold has not been adjusted for inflation since 1978, PolitiFact Ohio found that this does not change the facts or statistics as stated by Portman. The data also shows that many regulations result from laws passed by Congress or court orders, rather than presidential initiatives.

In conclusion, PolitiFact Ohio's analysis of the data confirms that the Obama administration has issued more major rules than the Clinton administration or the Bush administration during comparable times. Therefore, we rate Portman's claim True.

**The Hidden Truth Behind Portland's Levy: Where Does the Money Really Go?**

Imagine a system where millions of dollars are allocated to help the most vulnerable members of society, but a significant chunk of it disappears into a black hole of administrative costs. This is precisely what's happening with the Portland Children's Levy, a program that's been touted as a beacon of hope for low-income and at-risk children.

When supporters of the levy first pitched the idea to voters in 2002 and 2008, they made a promise: administrative costs would be capped at 5 percent of all money received from increased property taxes. Sounds like a noble endeavor, right? But what does it really mean?

According to the levy's annual audits, administrators have consistently met the 5 percent standard, but the devil's in the details. For instance, in the 2010-11 fiscal year, the fund brought in $12.9 million, but a whopping $560,000 was spent on administration – that's 4.3 percent of the total. And if that's not enough, the levy's administrators can carry over unused funds to the next year, effectively allowing them to exceed the 5 percent cap.

But what exactly constitutes administrative costs? According to the levy's spokeswoman, Mary Gay Broderick, it includes everything from salaries and benefits for staff to office supplies and computer costs. And it's not just the levy that's guilty of this – other groups, like the Portland Development Commission, have administrative rates of up to 13 percent.

So, is a 5 percent cap a reasonable expectation? The answer is unclear, and even City Commissioner Dan Saltzman can't recall how the figure was chosen. But what's certain is that voters deserve transparency and accountability when it comes to their tax dollars.

As the city gears up to put the arts tax on the ballot, it's time to ask the tough questions. Where will the money really go? Will it be used to fund programs that benefit the community, or will it disappear into a sea of administrative costs? The people of Portland deserve to know the truth.

A forensic photography expert at Syracuse University's Forensic and National Security Sciences Institute analyzed the photo and concluded that it was likely photoshopped. The expert stated that the original image of Johnson was shot at a press event and that the graphic design was applied to the image to make it appear as if Johnson was wearing the T-shirt with the message.

When contacted for comment, Miller's campaign spokesman, Todd Smith, dismissed the inquiry as "silly" and stated that the message of the T-shirt was what mattered, not the authenticity of the photo. However, Johnson's representative stated that the image shared by Miller was indeed photoshopped.

In conclusion, our investigation found that the photo posted by Miller was a product of photo manipulation, and we rate this photo post as False. Budget Debate Heats Up in Washington as GOP Unveils Spending Proposals

As the federal budget process gets underway, a key proposal from U.S. Rep. Tom Price, R-Roswell, is sparking debate over the nation's spending priorities. The House Budget Committee chairman unveiled his 2016 budget resolution last week, which aims to reduce spending by $5.5 trillion over the next 10 years to achieve a budget surplus by 2025.

The House narrowly approved a budget on Thursday that follows much of Price's blueprint but adds $38 billion in war funding. The original plan emphasizes spending cuts, with Price warning that interest payments on the nation's debt will soon surpass defense spending.

"Under current conditions, by 2023, interest payments on the nation's debt alone will be $722 billion," Price wrote in the budget blueprint. "That will be larger than the Congressional Budget Office's projected defense spending budget of $696 billion."

Budget analysts have questioned the accuracy of Price's claims, citing the potential for changes in the economy and global events. However, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) projections, which Price cites, do show a significant increase in interest payments on the national debt.

According to the CBO's January budget and economic outlook for 2015 to 2025, the nation's debt is projected to be about 2.6 percent of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 2023. This is the smallest deficit relative to economic output since 2007, but just under the 50-year historical average of 2.7 percent of GDP.

The CBO report projects that interest payments on the national debt will reach $722 billion in 2023, while defense spending is forecast to total $696 billion. However, if sequestration cuts are lifted, defense spending is projected to reach $752 billion in 2023, exceeding interest payments.

Laura Wheeler, a senior research associate at the Center for State and Local Finance at Georgia State University, noted that the CBO projections are not hard and fast expectations, but rather refined estimates based on known factors at a snapshot in time. She emphasized that many outside analysts prefer to examine the debt level compared with the GDP.

The debate over the nation's rising deficits has become a philosophical discussion about how to handle the concern. Price's claim that interest payments on the national debt will soon surpass defense spending is supported by the CBO projections, but the decision to compare military spending with debt is not a common way to benchmark projections.

PolitiFact Georgia has rated Price's claim True, citing the CBO projections as a credible source of information. However, the accuracy of the projections will depend on various factors, including changes in the economy and global events.

The Crushing Reality of America's Stagnant Wages

As former President Bill Clinton stood in Phoenix on March 20, pleading for his wife's support, he revealed a painful truth that resonates deeply with millions of Americans. The country's crippling gridlock is not the only source of frustration - it's the harsh reality that 80 percent of the American people have been left behind, struggling to make ends meet without a pay raise since the devastating crash of 2007.

The December 2007 recession ravaged Arizona's housing market, leaving a trail of destruction and wiping out countless construction jobs. It's a nightmare that many still live with today. Hillary Clinton echoed her husband's sentiments in a campaign advertisement, highlighting the fact that Americans haven't seen a real raise in 15 long, grueling years.

But what about the numbers? PolitiFact dug deeper, only to find that while there was a slight increase in weekly earnings between 2000 and 2015, median household income had actually plummeted between 1999 and 2014. It's a stark reminder that household income is a more complete measure of income growth, encompassing vital sources like Social Security and investments.

We spoke to experts who confirmed the heart-wrenching truth. The Economic Policy Institute, a leading think tank, analyzed data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and U.S. Census Bureau, revealing that real, inflation-adjusted wages stagnated for the bottom 80 percent of wage earners between 2007 and 2014. The only glimmer of hope came in 2015, when real wages increased by a paltry 1.7 percent - a fleeting reprieve courtesy of a one-time dip in inflation.

Other experts echoed Bill Clinton's claim, highlighting the crippling wage inequality that persists to this day. Bill Lester, an economic development professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, analyzed income data from 1973 to 2012 and found that wages for the bottom 80 percent either declined or stagnated between 2008 and 2012.

The verdict is clear: Bill Clinton's claim is a harsh but accurate reflection of America's stagnant wages. While there have been some minor increases in real wages and median weekly earnings, they come with asterisks - and a sobering reminder that millions of Americans continue to struggle to make ends meet. We rate Bill Clinton's claim as Mostly True, a painful acknowledgment of the crushing reality that America's economic recovery has left far too many behind.

A contentious debate has emerged over Deepwater Wind's plans to construct two wind energy projects off the coasts of Rhode Island and Massachusetts. Critics, including former Rhode Island Attorney General James O'Neil, have raised concerns about the cost and reliability of the proposed projects.

O'Neil has questioned the reliability of wind energy, stating that it is the most undependable form of renewable energy. However, experts in the field argue that wind energy is not inherently unreliable. According to Willett Kempton, a University of Delaware professor, wind turbines are generally more reliable than thermal plants, such as those powered by natural gas, coal, or nuclear energy.

Kempton points out that the availability of wind and daylight, which vary by location, is a more significant issue for renewable energy sources. He notes that wind can be predicted with a high degree of accuracy, and that the National Weather Service provides hourly forecasts of wind and cloud cover up to six days in advance.

Other experts have weighed in on the debate, highlighting the importance of dispatchability, which refers to a power plant's ability to quickly adjust its output to meet changing demand. Fossil fuel plants are generally more adept at dispatchability than wind or solar energy sources.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) has conducted a comprehensive analysis of various forms of electrical generation, including wind and solar energy. According to the EIA's latest report, wind power has a capacity factor of 37 percent, while solar panels generate electricity directly at a capacity factor of 25 percent. In contrast, geothermal energy has a capacity factor of 92 percent, while biomass and hydroelectric power have capacity factors of 83 percent and 52 percent, respectively.

In response to O'Neil's assertion that wind is the most undependable form of renewable energy, the EIA's data suggests that wind power is actually more reliable than solar energy on a nationwide basis. O'Neil has since stated that his opinion remains unchanged, but acknowledges that wind and solar energy are both relatively close in terms of reliability.

In conclusion, the debate over the reliability of wind energy highlights the complexities of the issue. While wind energy has its strengths and weaknesses, the available data suggests that it is not inherently unreliable. The actual dependability of wind energy will depend on various factors, including location, technology, and grid infrastructure.

According to the Oregon Department of Consumer and Business Services, average premium increases for 2010 ranged from 8 to 17 percent, with some Oregonians seeing increases of nearly 30 percent in 2008.

Moreover, the 1 percent tax is also funding a program that insures 80,000 Oregon children. Insuring these children may eventually lead to a slowdown of premium increases, although this may not provide immediate relief to families.
