Supporters of President Donald Trump have been making unsubstantiated allegations of widespread voter fraud in the recent election. One high-profile Republican ally, American Conservative Union chair Matt Schlapp, claimed that 9,000 Nevada ballots were fraudulently cast by nonresidents.

During a press conference on November 8, Schlapp stated that "we have literally 9,000 people who voted in this election who don't live in Nevada." He also cited the 9,000 figure on Fox News, claiming that many "non-Nevadans" had been caught illegally voting in the state. Schlapp has continued to repeat the claim since.

Schlapp's allegation received support from Trump, who tweeted that Nevada was "a cesspool of fake votes." However, there is no proof to support the claim that 9,000 people cast illegal ballots in Nevada after moving out of state.

The 9,000 figure is derived from a Trump campaign list, which included 3,062 instances of voter fraud stemming from cases in which people moved out of Nevada but still voted in the state. The list was based on a comparison of voter registration records and publicly available change-of-address records. However, the list alone does not prove that anyone had violated the law.

According to Nevada law, people who move within 30 days before an election can legally cast a ballot in their new state or their prior state of residence. Additionally, Nevadans who leave the state to attend college or other reasons can request a ballot.

The list from Trump's lawyers included addresses for Americans serving overseas in the military and their spouses, including some people who have since spoken out. The ACLU of Nevada said the list showed changes of address for people who moved to military bases, including at least 129 Army or Air Post Office addresses, 13 Fleet Post Offices, and 15 Diplomatic Post Offices.

Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford said that the list has been debunked as having included military personnel who are serving overseas and have the right to vote. He also noted that it could include Mormon missionaries and college students who are eligible to vote.

Clark County, which includes Las Vegas and nearly 75% of Nevada's population, has referred just three cases of potential fraud to the Nevada secretary of state's office. None of the three cases involved an ineligible voter from out of state.

Schlapp's claim relies on back-of-the-envelope math and some major assumptions, including the assumption that everyone who mailed in a ballot was ineligible to do so. There is no evidence to support the claim that 9,000 people cast illegal ballots in Nevada.

A spokesperson for the American Conservative Union said that Schlapp had projected that the number of people who illegally voted from outside Nevada was actually three times as large as the 3,062 people originally alleged. However, this claim is also unsubstantiated.

Nevada law does allow the residency of registered voters to be challenged, including for people who have moved. However, this would require an affidavit to be filed by the challenger with the county clerk in advance of the election.

In conclusion, Schlapp's claim that 9,000 people voted in Nevada who do not live in the state is unsubstantiated and lacks credible evidence. Our fact-checking rating is Pants on Fire!

Wisconsin U.S. Senate Candidate Tommy Thompson Claims Democrat Tammy Baldwin Supports Government-Controlled Health Care

In his bid to win a Wisconsin U.S. Senate seat and potentially shift control of the Senate to the Republican Party, Republican Tommy Thompson has repeatedly characterized Democrat Tammy Baldwin as supporting extreme health care policies.

During a September 27, 2012, appearance on WISN-AM in Milwaukee, Thompson focused on health care and stated that if Baldwin is elected, she would push for a national health care provision that would allow the government to make decisions on medicine, doctors, and hospitals.

PolitiFact National previously evaluated Thompson's claim that Baldwin wants to implement a "Medicare system for all," which was rated as Mostly True. However, Thompson's statement that Baldwin would have the federal government decide a patient's private medical matters is a more extreme assertion.

Thompson's language is reminiscent of the 2010 Lie of the Year, which claimed that President Barack Obama's health care reform law constituted a "government takeover of health care." However, the Affordable Care Act relies largely on the free market, with employers continuing to provide health insurance to most Americans through private insurance companies.

Thompson's campaign spokeswoman, Lisa Boothe, cited two legislative efforts to support Thompson's statement, including Baldwin's support for Obama's reform law and her support for a single-payer health care system. Boothe argued that the reform law "puts the government in between a patient and their doctor in Medicare" and leaves an unaccountable board of 15 unelected bureaucrats in charge of rationing care and limiting access to health care.

However, PolitiFact National has reported that the reform law does not outline a dramatic, structural overhaul of the program, and the board does not make decisions for individuals. Additionally, a single-payer system refers to a health care system in which the government pays for all health care services but is not involved in the delivery of health care.

Health policy experts contacted by PolitiFact National were unpersuaded by Thompson's claim. They noted that the health care reform law will put more people into private insurance plans, allowing them to choose from among private plans, and that a single-payer system would not necessarily result in the government making decisions for patients.

Our analysis

Thompson's statement that Baldwin supports a law "in which government will take over your decisions on medicine, on doctors and on hospitals" is not supported by evidence. Experts were unpersuaded by his claim, and we rate his statement False.

The same report estimates that 0.7 percent of U.S. minors aged 13 to 17 identify as transgender, which breaks out to about 2.1-in-300 individuals.

The numbers are staggering, but it's not just about numbers; it's about people's lives. The uncertainty and fear that comes with being transgender is palpable.

As Smith said, "We're all over the place, we're your friends and your neighbors." But what happens when we're forced to hide who we are, when we're forced to live in fear of being discovered? The proposed Texas law is a direct attack on the very essence of who we are. It's a reminder that we're not seen, we're not heard, and we're not valued.

The truth is, there's no direct national count of individuals identifying as transgender, but the estimates are clear: we're here, we're real, and we deserve to be treated with dignity and respect. Texas Power Grid's Unorthodox Layout Raises Questions About Federal Regulation

A recent winter blackout has highlighted the unique structure of the Texas power grid, which serves as the only standalone grid in the continental United States. This setup has led some to speculate that the state's aversion to federal regulation is the primary reason for its isolation.

The Texas grid, managed by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), accounts for more than 90% of the state's electric load. However, the history of the grid's formation suggests that a desire to avoid federal oversight played a significant role in its creation.

In 1935, the Federal Power Act was signed into law, establishing the Federal Power Commission to regulate electricity sales that crossed state lines. In response, Texas electric companies and energy authorities sought to prevent federal interference by keeping the power grid within the state's borders. This move, dubbed the "Electric Alamo," allowed them to avoid federal regulations, as the Federal Power Commission only had jurisdiction over interstate sales.

A written agreement, binding Texas utilities to intrastate operation, was a key component of this policy. The agreement was formalized in a 1995 court account by U.S. Circuit Judge Richard D. Cudahy, who described it as a deliberate attempt to maintain traditional Texas independence.

The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) was established in 1970 to oversee the grid, which remains outside the reach of federal regulators. Despite several attempts to integrate the Texas grid into the broader U.S. power system, ERCOT has consistently maintained its independence.

In 1976, a Texas utility company briefly allowed power to flow to an Oklahoma property, known as the "Midnight Connection," in an attempt to bring the state under federal jurisdiction. However, the case was ultimately decided in ERCOT's favor, and the grid remained independent.

ERCOT has promoted its freedom from federal regulation in promotional videos, with CEO Bill Magness stating that the state's energy independence has been "jealously guarded" by policymakers and the industry.

However, this independence has come with drawbacks. By isolating its grid, Texas has limited its ability to import power from other energy systems, said Carey King, assistant director of the Energy Institute at UT Austin. While ERCOT has two minor ties to the Eastern grid, these connections are not sufficient to meet demand in the event of a blackout.

In conclusion, the history of the Texas power grid supports the claim that a fear of federal regulation drove the state's decision to maintain a standalone grid.

At a campaign event in western North Carolina on July 4, Lt. Gov. Dan Forest, the Republican candidate for governor, expressed skepticism about the effectiveness of face coverings during the coronavirus pandemic. Forest, who is running against incumbent Democrat Roy Cooper, claimed that scientific evidence does not support mask mandates.

Forest stated that multiple comprehensive studies have shown that masks are ineffective against viruses. However, his assertion ignores recent research and federal health guidance that suggests mask-wearing can reduce the spread of COVID-19.

According to Forest, the evidence comes from studies conducted in controlled environments, which have consistently shown that masks are not effective in preventing the spread of viruses. However, experts have pointed out that this statement is not entirely accurate.

In fact, recent studies have shown that mask-wearing can help slow down the spread of COVID-19. Virologist Dr. Anthony Fauci and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have stated that while masks alone cannot guarantee protection from the virus, they can help reduce the risk of transmission.

When asked to provide sources to support Forest's claim, his campaign cited a study published in the New England Journal of Medicine in April. However, the authors of the study later clarified that their intention was to push for more widespread masking, not less.

The study, which examined the effectiveness of masks in healthcare settings, found that masks offered little protection against infection in passing encounters in public spaces. However, the authors noted that sustained interactions within closed environments posed a higher risk of transmission.

The Forest campaign also cited a 2015 study published in the U.S. National Library of Medicine, which examined the use of non-pharmaceutical interventions to reduce the spread of the flu. The study found that the efficacy of masks was unclear due to design flaws in the studies examined.

However, more recent studies have shown that masks can help prevent the spread of COVID-19. A study published in the U.S. National Library of Medicine in April found that surgical face masks significantly reduced the detection of viral RNA in aerosols and droplets. Another study published in The Royal Society in June found that facemask use by the public could make a major contribution to reducing the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Rachel Graham, an assistant professor of epidemiology at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, noted that a study out of Germany found that a mask mandate decreased the COVID-19 growth rate by about 40%. Graham stated that while masks may not eliminate transmission entirely, they can reduce the risk of infection.

The CDC has also updated its guidance on mask-wearing, recommending that nearly everyone wear a face covering in public settings. PolitiFact has reported on the effectiveness of masks, citing experts who say that coverings can effectively reduce the spread of COVID-19 when combined with other prevention methods such as frequent hand washing and social distancing.

In conclusion, while Forest's claim that masks "do not work" against viruses is inaccurate, it is based on a misunderstanding of the scientific evidence. Recent research has shown that masks can reduce the risk of spreading COVID-19, and experts recommend their use in public settings to slow the spread of the virus.

Confederate-themed posts have been circulating on social media in the wake of the Unite the Right march in Charlottesville, Va. The march was sparked by efforts to remove a statue of Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee and included some marchers carrying Confederate symbols.

One such post claims that "at the PEAK of slavery in 1860, only 1.4% of Americans owned slaves. What your history books doesn’t tell you is that 3,000 blacks owned a total of 20,000 slaves the same year." However, an examination of the data reveals that the post is misleading.

According to the 1860 Census, which is the primary source of data about slaves and slaveholding in 1860, slaves accounted for 12.6 percent of the national population. However, to accurately measure slaveholding, experts say that a more detailed analysis of family or household units in states that allowed slavery is necessary.

Using Census data, historians have calculated that 4.9 percent of people in slaveholding states owned slaves, 19.9 percent of family units in those states owned slaves, and 24.9 percent of households owned slaves. These figures are significantly higher than the 1.4 percent cited in the social media post.

Regarding the claim that 3,000 blacks owned a total of 20,000 slaves in 1860, historians were unable to find hard data to support or debunk this figure. However, research by Carter G. Woodson, an African-American historian, found that in 1830, a total of 3,776 free Negroes owned 12,907 slaves. With three decades of population growth, it is plausible that the number of black-owned slaves could have grown to 20,000 by 1860.

While the 20,000 number is not necessarily inaccurate, it represents a tiny fraction of all slaves held in the United States in 1860, specifically one half of 1 percent. Additionally, many of these black "slaveholders" likely "owned" family members whom they had purchased to become free, due to the prevailing laws in many slaveholding states.

In conclusion, the viral post's claims about the extent of slavery in 1860 are largely inaccurate. The number of families that owned slaves was significantly higher than 1.4 percent, and the number of black-owned slaves was a tiny fraction of all slaves held in the United States.

A recent advertisement from Hillary Clinton's campaign has sparked a controversy over which candidate is more likely to stand up to the energy industry. The ad targets Barack Obama, claiming that he has accepted significant donations from individuals employed by oil companies.

The Clinton ad begins by referencing a statement made by Obama, in which he claims not to take money from oil companies. However, the ad's narrator notes that corporations are prohibited by law from directly donating to political candidates, and instead points out that Obama accepted $200,000 from executives and employees of oil companies.

It is worth noting that Obama would have been more accurate if he had specified that he does not accept money from oil company lobbyists or political action committees. In a subsequent ad, Obama made this distinction, which was found to be mostly true.

An analysis by the nonpartisan Center for Responsive Politics confirms that Obama did accept $222,309 from executives and employees of oil companies. While it is true that these donations could come from anyone within the company, from the CEO to the janitor, the individuals who donate are required to list their occupation and employer.

In contrast, Clinton's campaign has not highlighted the fact that she also accepted significant donations from executives and employees of oil companies, totaling $309,363, according to the Center for Responsive Politics. Additionally, Clinton accepted about $442,800 from energy lobbyists, although not all of these donations are from the oil and gas industry.

Despite these discrepancies, the Clinton ad's statement that Obama accepted money from employees of oil companies is accurate, and we rate the ad's claim as True.

A Viral Facebook Post Attributes a Misquoted Thomas Jefferson Statement to Him

A recent Facebook post claiming that Thomas Jefferson stated that freedom is lost gradually from "uninterested, uninformed and uninvolved people" has garnered significant attention, with over 19,000 shares since September 3. However, an investigation by PolitiFact found no evidence to support this claim.

Thomas Jefferson, the third U.S. president and Founding Father, is frequently quoted online, but unfortunately, this often leads to misattributions. Researchers at the University of Virginia Press, which works in conjunction with Founders Online, have stated that they have found no evidence of the quote in Jefferson's writings or speeches.

David Sewell, managing editor of Digital Initiatives at the organization, noted that the style and phrasing of the quote are uncharacteristic of Jefferson's writing, and a search of Founders Online reveals that he rarely used the words "uninterested" or "uninvolved." Additionally, these words were less common in the 18th century, particularly in the sense of "not active in affairs/politics," which is a more modern usage.

Previous fact-checks have highlighted a spurious quotations list compiled on Jefferson's estate website, Monticello.org. Although the statement in question is not included on this list, research librarians at Monticello were unable to locate the quote in any of Jefferson's writings or print media.

Lisa Francavilla, managing editor for the Thomas Jefferson Papers at the International Center for Jefferson Studies, stated that the quote is being widely disseminated online without any confirmed source. "We have been unable to find any source that confirms that these are words written or spoken by Thomas Jefferson," Francavilla wrote. "It is therefore what we call'spurious' or'misattributed.'"

PolitiFact rates this claim as False.

A Democratic-led plan to reduce carbon emissions and expand cleaner energy sources has sparked concerns that it could make the United States vulnerable to reliance on China, according to some Republicans.

At a hearing on the CLEAN Future Act, the Democrats' climate bill, Rep. Cathy Rodgers, R-Wash., expressed concerns that the plan could compromise U.S. energy security. Rodgers, the ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce committee, stated that 90% of solar panels, 80% of wind machines, and 90% of rare earth minerals for batteries are sourced from Asia or China.

While Rodgers specifically highlighted China's dominance in these areas, her statement also included other Asian countries, such as Japan and South Korea. The geopolitical implications of the plan were a key concern for Rodgers.

To assess the validity of Rodgers' claims, the numbers were examined for each of the three renewable power systems she mentioned. The data revealed that while China does have a significant role in producing key materials, the reliance on Chinese companies is not as extensive as Rodgers suggested.

For solar panels, China produces over 90% of the silicon wafers, a critical component. However, a report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies found that the United States is most exposed in the solar sector, followed by energy storage and then wind. The report highlighted China's key role in producing the parts that go into solar panels.

In 2019, the latest year for which data is available, China accounted for less than 6% of the solar panels imported to the United States, measured by their generation capacity. Malaysia was the largest supplier, representing about 38% of all shipments, followed by Vietnam with 25%.

However, many of the Malaysian-based solar factories are Chinese-owned, and the wafers primarily come from China. This concentration in the supply chain is a concern, according to David Sandalow, a veteran of the Clinton and Obama administrations now at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy.

Regarding wind power equipment, Rodgers' claim that 80% of wind machines are from China or Asia is not accurate. While China does provide a fifth of all the imported blades, it does not rank in the top five among countries selling to the United States for towers. China also accounts for about 5% of imports for wind-powered generating systems.

However, wind turbines do rely on powerful magnets, which require compounds that tend to come from China. China dominates the production of rare earth minerals, which are essential for wind power and electric vehicles. The Democratic Republic of the Congo dominates the cobalt supply, while Australia and Chile produce most of the world's lithium.

The U.S. government has been working to diversify its supply base and shrink its reliance on Chinese materials. In 2019, the Trump administration triggered the Defense Production Act, and the Pentagon signed contracts with domestic suppliers. The U.S. government now has a stockpile of 600 tons of neodymium, and research is underway to develop rare-earth-free magnets.

In conclusion, while China does have a significant role in producing key materials for renewable energy, the reliance on Chinese companies is not as extensive as Rodgers suggested. The U.S. government has been working to diversify its supply base, and the current clean-energy policy focuses on weaning the U.S. off its dependence on China.

The Trump Administration has signaled a possible shift in its stance on recreational marijuana in states that have legalized the substance, such as California. This change in approach could mark a departure from the Obama Administration's more permissive policy.

White House press secretary Sean Spicer stated on February 23, 2017, that the federal government would enforce the law regarding recreational marijuana, despite the substance being legalized in certain states. Spicer expressed the belief that there would be "greater enforcement" of federal laws on the matter.

The next day, California Lt. Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote a letter to President Trump, urging him to follow the hands-off approach to marijuana that he claimed Trump had promised during his campaign. Newsom pointed to a Quinnipiac poll that found 71% of US voters believed the government should not interfere with states that have legalized marijuana.

Newsom also referenced his own role in helping to write California's Proposition 64, which legalized recreational marijuana in the state. He is running for California governor in 2018.

To determine whether Newsom's claim was accurate, PolitiFact researched Trump's statements on marijuana during his campaign. According to Trump's comments, he stated that the issue of marijuana legalization should be left to the states.

In a July 2016 television interview with KUSA-TV in Colorado, Trump said he believed marijuana legalization should be up to the states, stating, "I think it's up to the states, yeah. I'm a states person. I think it should be up to the states, absolutely."

In a March 2016 radio interview with WWJ Newsradio 950 in Michigan, Trump stated that marijuana legalization should be a state decision, saying, "I think it certainly has to be a state — I have not smoked it — it's got to be a state decision."

Additionally, at a campaign rally in Sparks, Nevada, on October 29, 2015, Trump said that marijuana legalization should be left to the states, stating, "I think medical should happen — right? Don't we agree? I think so. And then I really believe we should leave it up to the states. It should be a state situation... but I believe that the legalization of marijuana – other than for medical because I think medical, you know I know people that are very, very sick and for whatever reason the marijuana really helps them - … but in terms of marijuana and legalization, I think that should be a state issue, state-by-state."

However, in a February 2016 Fox News interview, Trump expressed concerns about the impact of recreational marijuana in Colorado, stating, "But what you are talking about (with recreational marijuana), perhaps not. It's causing a lot of problems out there."

U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions has also expressed opposition to marijuana legalization, stating that it remains a violation of federal law to distribute marijuana, regardless of whether a state has legalized it.

In conclusion, PolitiFact found that Newsom's claim that Trump "committed to honoring states' rights when it comes to marijuana legalization" during his campaign was accurate, based on Trump's own statements on the issue.

On May 29, 2011, Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz, D-Fla., criticized a proposal by Representative Paul Ryan, R-Wis., to reform Medicare. The proposal, which was passed by the House in a near party-line vote, aims to make significant changes to the Medicare program.

Under the Ryan plan, Medicare would remain unchanged for individuals 55 and older. However, new beneficiaries would be insured by private insurance companies rather than the federal government, although they would receive "premium support" - financial assistance from the government for buying insurance. The plan would gradually raise the Medicare eligibility age to 67 and provide smaller premium support to high earners.

The Ryan plan would also establish an "exchange" - a virtual marketplace - where private insurance plans would be sold. These plans would comply with standards set by the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, which administers the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program. Medicare payments would rise, but not at a rate expected to keep pace with the growth in medical costs.

Wasserman Schultz criticized the Ryan plan, stating that it would "end Medicare as we know it" and leave younger individuals to find private health insurance on their own. However, critics have argued that the plan does not allow insurance companies to deny coverage or drop individuals with pre-existing conditions.

An examination of the Ryan plan reveals that it does not permit insurance companies to deny coverage based on pre-existing conditions. The plan's language states that health plans participating in the Medicare Exchange would agree to offer insurance to all Medicare beneficiaries, preventing "cherry-picking" and ensuring that the sickest and highest-cost beneficiaries receive coverage.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) has analyzed the plan and concluded that insurers participating in the revamped Medicare program would not be able to deny insurance for pre-existing conditions. The CBO's description of the plan notes that beneficiaries would choose among competing private insurance plans, which would have to comply with a standard for benefits set by the Office of Personnel Management.

Some critics have suggested that insurers could still find ways to circumvent the protections for pre-existing conditions. However, others argue that the same criticism could be applied to the Affordable Care Act passed by the Democratic-controlled Congress.

While the Ryan plan may not be ideal for individuals with pre-existing conditions, it is clear that the plan does not allow insurance companies to deny coverage based on these conditions. Therefore, Wasserman Schultz's statement that the Ryan plan would allow insurance companies to deny coverage and drop individuals with pre-existing conditions is inaccurate.

In conclusion, the Ryan plan is a complex proposal that aims to reform Medicare. While it has its flaws, it does not allow insurance companies to deny coverage based on pre-existing conditions. Further analysis and debate are necessary to fully understand the implications of the plan.

The mailer claims that Adams "voted twice to approve $8 billion in Obama stimulus spending." However, a closer examination of the issue reveals a more nuanced situation.

The issue is further complicated by the fact that many Florida legislators, including Republicans, voted for the state budgets that contained stimulus money. Mica's mailer has been criticized for being misleading and failing to provide an accurate comparison.

In conclusion, the facts suggest that Mica's claim that Obama counted on Adams to approve stimulus spending is not accurate. **The Crushing Reality Behind Keystone XL: A Meager 35 Permanent Jobs**

The debate over the Keystone XL pipeline has been raging on, with proponents touting it as a jobs creator. But is it really? Liberal CNN Crossfire host Van Jones says no, and he's got the numbers to back it up. In a recent episode, Jones blasted the pipeline's supposed job-creating abilities, saying that the actual numbers are a far cry from what supporters claim.

"We're constantly being told that Keystone is going to create all these jobs," Jones said, his voice dripping with frustration. "But when you look at the actual numbers, it's a joke. 3,900 temporary jobs in construction, and a whopping 35 permanent jobs. That's it."

Conservative activist Ralph Reed shot back, citing a report by the U.S. State Department that claims the project will create 42,000 jobs. But Jones isn't buying it. And neither are the facts. The State Department's own report says that the pipeline will create 42,100 jobs during construction, but that's a different story altogether. The real question is, what happens after construction is complete?

The answer is devastating. According to the report, the pipeline will only provide jobs for about 35 permanent employees and 15 temporary contractors. That's it. No more, no less. These jobs will be scattered along the pipeline route, with some employees working in Canada and others in the U.S.

The impact on local communities will be minimal, with little to no effect on housing, property taxes, or service industries. And let's be real, the contractors will only be needed for specialized support, not for any meaningful, long-term work.

The reality is, the Keystone XL pipeline is a massive construction project that will create temporary jobs, but once it's done, the impact will be negligible. Jones is right, and it's time to stop pretending that this pipeline is anything more than a meager jobs creator.

**Our Ruling: Jones is right, and the numbers are heartbreaking. The Keystone XL pipeline will only create 35 permanent jobs.**

Democratic gubernatorial nominee Bill White has vowed to tighten rules restricting state employees from working as lobbyists, citing the revolving door between the governor's office and the lobbying industry.

During a speech in the North Texas town of Crowell on Aug. 14, White noted that most of Governor Perry's top staffers have a background in lobbying. White was more specific in an ethics reform proposal he released in April, stating that five of the seven chiefs of staff Perry has had during his gubernatorial tenure were lobbyists.

State law regulates lobbying, which is defined as direct communications with members of state agencies, the legislative or executive branch of state government, to influence legislation or administrative action. This includes the offices of the governor.

White proposed prohibiting the governor's senior staff from working on issues related to their former employment for two years and prohibiting them from lobbying the governor's office or their state agency for two years after departing.

Mark Miner, a spokesman for Perry's campaign, has said that the governor has some of the toughest ethics policies anywhere in the country, citing a one-year lobbying ban on the governor's office and a legislative session.

The validity of White's claim was investigated by reviewing the governor's chiefs of staff and the Texas Ethics Commission's online database of registered lobbyists. The database only dates back to 1998, so the investigation also involved reaching out to the former chiefs of staff themselves.

He was a vice president of Centene Corp., a St. Louis-based health insurance company, and registered as a lobbyist as a standard precaution for having any contacts with legislators.

Toomey was chief of staff from December 2002 to September 2004 and was registered as a lobbyist from 1990 to 2002 and again from 2004 to present. He had more than 30 clients listed in 2002, including Merck and Philip Morris, and reported a minimum of $800,000 and a maximum of $1.5 million in prospective compensation in 2010.

Sullivan has been chief of staff since July 2009 and was registered as a lobbyist from 2002 to 2009. He had seven clients listed to his name on the ethics website in 2009, including HNTP Corp., a toll-road engineering company.

Delisi, another chief of staff, has been with Perry since he was lieutenant governor and served as his chief of staff until June 2007. She told investigators that she has never been a registered lobbyist, and a review of news clips and lobbyist registries confirmed as much.

Newby and Kimbrough, two other chiefs of staff, also denied being lobbyists, and a review of the ethics commission database did not find any evidence to the contrary.

The investigation found that White's statement about five of the seven chiefs of staff being lobbyists was true.

In fall 2007, the state rented a home for the governor and his wife, Anita, approximately 11 miles southwest of downtown Austin to facilitate renovations to the Governor's Mansion. White then called on Perry to "set a budget-cutting example for other state employees and move out."

Kay Bailey Hutchison, R-Texas, also supported this information, stating that Perry "lives in a luxury house that costs taxpayers $10,000 a month." The lease for the house at 8113 Hickory Creek Drive, which was appraised by the Travis Central Appraisal District at $1.1 million in 2008, was initially set for one year starting Oct. 1, 2007.

The lease was renewed in fall 2008 through October 2011 with a reduced rent of $9,000. As of this April, the state has paid $290,700 in rent. If we include the eight months remaining in Perry's current term, the total rental payments would be $362,700. We have confirmed that White's calculation is accurate, excluding other housing-related expenses.

For comparison, the ancillary costs of living at the Governor's Mansion in 2007 totaled more than $330,000. However, it is essential to note that these costs were likely influenced by the fact that the mansion needed renovation at the time. We do not have an exact comparison of the ancillary costs of living at the rental residence.

In conclusion, White's statement about the expected rent costs for the Perrys to reside in suburban Austin is accurate. We rate White's statement as True.

New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman is leading a lawsuit against the Trump administration over its decision to rescind the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program. Schneiderman and 15 other attorneys general argue that the move is discriminatory and that the program itself has not been ruled unconstitutional.

The DACA program, introduced by the Obama administration in 2012, protects from deportation immigrants who came to the United States as children and live here illegally. U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced on September 5 that the program would be ended.

Schneiderman and other attorneys general contend that the administration's action discriminates against Mexican immigrants, who account for 78 percent of DACA recipients. Schneiderman stated on MSNBC's The Rachel Maddow Show that Trump has "flagrantly displayed an anti-Latino, particularly anti-Mexican discriminatory animus."

Schneiderman emphasized that the program has been successful and that there is no legitimate reason to shut it down, citing that no court has held it unconstitutional. This assertion is supported by experts, who note that DACA's constitutionality has not been determined by courts.

The DACA program was created by a 2012 memo issued by Janet Napolitano, then-Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security. The memo outlined prosecutorial discretion to prioritize the removal of immigrants who meet the department's priorities and protect from deportation young immigrants who meet specific criteria.

While some have argued that creating DACA through the executive branch rather than the legislative process is an overreach of executive power, experts agree that no court has ruled on the constitutionality of the program. Anil Kalhan, an associate professor of law at Drexel University, stated that there has been no court decision holding that DACA itself is unconstitutional.

A lawsuit to challenge the 2012 DACA was dismissed for lack of standing, and the decision was upheld by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. Shoba Sivaprasad Wadhia, a law professor and director of the Center for Immigrants' Rights Clinic at Pennsylvania State University, noted that no court has ruled DACA 2012 as unconstitutional.

Other experts from the University of California also agree that courts have not stricken down DACA as unconstitutional. Amy Spitalnick, spokeswoman for Schneiderman, stated that it is a "straightforward fact" that no court has declared DACA unconstitutional.

A related case involving an expanded version of DACA and another deportation reprieve program, Deferred Action for Parents of Americans and Lawful Permanent Residents (DAPA), was temporarily enjoined by a federal district court in Texas. However, the court's ruling was not based on constitutional grounds, but rather on a conclusion that the Obama administration should have used notice and comment rule-making to institute the policy.

PolitiFact has rated Schneiderman's statement "No court has held (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals) unconstitutional" as True, citing that there is no court ruling on the constitutionality of the program.

Voter ID Laws and Racial Turnout: A Complex Debate

A recent statement by Attorney General Eric Holder suggesting that racial animus is fueling criticism of President Obama has been dismissed as "political posturing" by Wall Street Journal columnist Jason L. Riley. Riley, a prominent commentator on racial issues, argued that Holder's comments are an attempt to motivate minority voters by claiming that voter ID laws suppress the black vote.

Riley made his comments on Fox News' The Kelly File, a day after Holder's remarks on ABC's This Week. Riley stated that Democrats are concerned about minority turnout in November and are using fear-mongering tactics to motivate voters. He cited data from the U.S. Census Bureau, which shows that black voter turnout exceeded white voter turnout in the 2012 elections, even in states with the strictest voter ID laws.

The Census Bureau's 2013 report indicates that black voter turnout was 66.2 percent, surpassing the white voter turnout rate of 64.1 percent by 2.1 percentage points in the 2012 elections. However, experts note that the impact of voter ID laws on voter turnout is difficult to gauge due to various factors that influence voting behavior.

In states with the strictest voter ID laws, such as Missouri, Tennessee, and Georgia, black voter turnout was higher than white voter turnout in the 2012 elections. However, experts caution that this does not necessarily mean that voter ID laws do not suppress or attempt to suppress the minority vote.

The impact of voter ID laws is challenging to measure due to the complexity of voting behavior. According to Alex Keyssar, a political scientist at Harvard University, it is difficult to track why individuals do not show up to vote, making it hard to determine the consequences of voter ID laws.

The newness of the legislation and the fact that many laws were not in place in the 2012 elections make it even more challenging to assess their impact. John Hansen, a political scientist at the University of Chicago, notes that one election does not make a pattern and that more time is needed to measure the effects of these laws.

The high turnout of black voters in 2012 may be attributed to President Obama's presence on the ballot, according to Hansen and Keyssar. In future elections, when Obama's name will not appear on the ballot, and the laws are in place, the rates may tell a different story.

Erin O'Brien, a political scientist at the University of Massachusetts Boston, suggests that the increased black voter rates in 2012 could be an unintended consequence or a "backlash effect." The stricter voter ID laws may have actually motivated minorities, who were trying to suppress their vote.

The debate over voter ID laws and their impact on racial turnout is ongoing. Critics argue that these laws are an attempt to suppress minority votes, while proponents claim that they are necessary to prevent voter fraud.

In conclusion, while the data shows that black voter turnout exceeded white voter turnout in the 2012 elections, even in states with the strictest voter ID laws, the impact of these laws on voter turnout is complex and difficult to measure.

Austin City Council Candidate's Claim About Council Representation Examined

A recent statement made by Max Nofziger, a South Austin resident running for a seat on the Austin City Council, has sparked interest in the council's composition. When asked about the city's voting system, Nofziger expressed a preference for a mix of council members elected at-large and from single-member districts. He also stated that there is currently no one from South Austin on the council.

In the League of Women Voters of the Austin Area's "Voters Guide," Nofziger is quoted as saying, "Currently, there is no one from South Austin on the (Austin City) Council!" To verify this claim, we reviewed a January 23 article in the Austin American-Statesman, which reported on Austin Mayor Lee Leffingwell's proposal to reorganize the council.

According to the article, the current council composition includes three members living in or near downtown, two living in East Austin, one in Hyde Park, and the mayor, Leffingwell, residing in northwest Austin. Notably, the article stated that none of the council members live south of the Colorado River, which separates South Austin from the rest of the city.

We contacted Matt Curtis, the mayor's communications director, to verify the current council members' addresses. Curtis stated that, contrary to the article, some council members do live in areas other than those previously reported. For example, Sheryl Cole resides in Wilshire Woods, Laura Morrison lives in Old West Austin, Chris Riley is downtown, Randy Shade lives in Clarksville, and Bill Spelman hails from Hyde Park.

Curtis also provided information on the addresses of council members who have left their positions. He stated that the last South Austinites to serve on the council were Betty Dunkerley and Jennifer Kim, who completed their terms in June 2008.

Upon further review, we confirmed that Nofziger's statement about the lack of South Austin representation on the council is accurate.

Democratic Congresswoman Judy Chu of Los Angeles County made a statement regarding the GOP health care bill, which narrowly passed the U.S. House on May 4, 2017. In a press release, Chu stated that the legislation "would once again allow being a rape or domestic violence victim to be a pre-existing condition."

Chu and all other Democrats in the House opposed the bill, which has an uncertain future in the U.S. Senate. Fact-checking organizations, including PolitiFact and The Washington Post Fact Checker, have reviewed similar claims made in headlines and blogs. These fact-checkers have rated the statements "Mostly False" and described them as "bombastic" and "misleading."

PolitiFact noted that some blogs have changed their headlines or issued corrections in response to the fact-checking. In a written statement on May 10, 2017, Chu maintained her claim, stating that while fact-checkers pointed out that several conditions must be met before a state can waive certain protections, the fact remains that the American Health Care Act (AHCA) has made it possible for insurance companies to charge higher prices to people with pre-existing conditions.

PolitiFact Wisconsin summarized its findings, stating that the GOP bill does not single out any specific medical event or diagnosis as a pre-existing condition. However, conditions stemming from a sexual assault or domestic violence, such as post-traumatic stress disorder or certain sexually transmitted diseases, could be judged to be a pre-existing condition. States would have the option to allow insurers to charge higher prices to people with an existing condition, potentially making coverage unaffordable.

Experts, including Linda Blumberg of the Urban Institute, have pointed out that the Republican bill does not change what constitutes a pre-existing condition. Instead, it allows states to consider pre-existing conditions when setting premium costs. This could make insurance unaffordable for those with pre-existing conditions, including victims of sexual assault who may need to take medication or seek treatment.

Kathryn Votava, president of health care consulting company Goodcare, noted that the lack of transparency in the bill could lead to different policies from state to state, making it difficult for consumers to determine their eligibility for insurance. According to DeMint, Obey's partial earmark ban would not address the majority of earmarks, which he described as a "fig leaf, not real reform." The controversy surrounding earmarks has gained momentum in recent years, particularly in light of the massive budget deficit and several high-profile ethics investigations.

In February, the House ethics committee cleared seven members of the defense spending panel accused of awarding earmarks to companies whose executives and lobbyists donated to their campaigns. Although the members were cleared, the ethics committee noted that there was a perception among corporate donors that their contributions influenced a legislator's decision to award an earmark.

In response to these concerns, Rep. Obey initiated a ban on budget earmarks to private, for-profit companies on March 10, 2010. The move was hailed by several government watchdog groups as a meaningful step towards earmark reform.

"For-profit company earmarks are ground zero for pay-to-play," said Steve Ellis of the nonpartisan Taxpayers for Common Sense. However, DeMint's claim that Obey's ban would not affect 90% of earmarks has sparked debate.

According to Obey's calculation, the ban on earmarks to for-profit companies would have eliminated about 1,000 earmarks this year, totaling approximately $1.7 billion. In contrast, Taxpayers for Common Sense estimated that there were 9,499 earmarks this fiscal year, totaling $15.9 billion.

This puts the number of earmarks not going to for-profits close to DeMint's 90% figure. Democrats do not dispute the statistic but argue that DeMint's implication and follow-up comment are misleading.

"The political reality right now is that the public has lost some confidence in this institution, and one of the reasons is the past abuses of the earmark process," Obey said. Earmarks for profit-making companies are "the most vulnerable place" for abuse in the system, he added.

House Republicans have taken a more drastic approach, announcing that their members would renounce all earmarks for the rest of the year. In contrast, Senate Appropriations panel chair Daniel Inouye, D-Hawaii, has expressed skepticism about the ban, arguing that it would cede congressional authority to the executive branch.

Sen. DeMint has vowed to force a Senate vote on a proposal to put a one-year moratorium on all earmarks. He argues that the Senate should prioritize balancing the budget over pork-barrel spending. However, Rep. Obey has countered that banning all earmarks would make Congress a "rubber stamp" of the executive branch.

Ellis, of Taxpayers for Common Sense, has suggested that a one-year moratorium is a good starting point but that Congress needs a long-term solution to its spending protocol. He argues that earmarks are often based on the political muscle of their sponsors rather than project merit.

In conclusion, while DeMint's statement that Obey's ban on earmarks to for-profits would not affect 90% of earmarks is accurate, the implications and consequences of this proposal remain a subject of debate.

**The Devastating Truth About Prescription Drug Prices in America**

Imagine paying $215 for a medication that costs a mere $60 in other countries. It's a harsh reality that millions of Americans face every day due to the exorbitant prices of prescription drugs. Sen. Bernie Sanders has been vocal about this issue, and it's time to shine a light on the truth.

During the Democratic debate, Sanders rattled off a list of problems with the U.S. health care system, including the staggering cost of prescription drugs. But what's behind these sky-high prices? We dug deeper to find out.

According to the International Federation of Health Plans, the U.S. pays far more for prescription drugs than other countries, including England, the Netherlands, Spain, Switzerland, and Canada. For example, Nexium, a medication used to treat acid reflux, costs an average of $215 in the U.S., compared to $60 or less in other countries.

Experts warn that the prices are not only high but also vary wildly in the U.S. "There's nowhere that pays the same price as America," said Tom Sackville, the federation's CEO. "Anything above the average is quite unjustified. When you get up to the 95th percentile, you're talking grand robbery."

Studies have consistently shown that the U.S. pays more for prescription drugs than other countries. A 2013 study published in the journal Health Affairs found that U.S. prices were consistently higher than in the UK, Switzerland, Germany, France, Canada, and Australia.

But why do prices vary so much in the U.S.? The answer lies in the way the health care system is structured. Big customers, like countries with socialized medicine, can negotiate lower prices. However, in the U.S., hospitals, wholesalers, and insurance companies all do their own negotiations, leading to a fragmented market with high prices.

The pharmaceutical industry claims that it needs the extra income to fund research for new drugs. However, experts argue that Americans are essentially financing research for the rest of the world, while paying exorbitant prices for their own medications.

Amitava Dasgupta, a clinical toxicologist at the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, puts it bluntly: "The U.S. subsidizes research for the world. But I would look at that as philanthropy."

In conclusion, Sen. Sanders' claim that the U.S. pays the highest prices in the world for prescription drugs is a harsh reality that millions of Americans face every day. While there are some exceptions, studies support Sanders' claim, and the differences in price can be dramatic due to the splintered nature of the U.S. health care system. We rate his statement Mostly True, but the truth is far from comforting.

Portland's claim to be the most sustainable city in America has sparked debate over the effectiveness of its public transit system, particularly the MAX light rail. One common criticism is that the trains often appear to be empty, leading some to question their usefulness.

However, a recent advertisement by TriMet, the agency responsible for Portland's public transit, included a statistic that challenged this perception: "MAX carries 30 percent of evening rush hour commuters traveling from Downtown on the Sunset and Banfield freeways." The advertisement also featured a photograph of bumper-to-bumper freeway traffic alongside a MAX train cruising down the tracks.

The claim sparked curiosity, and we sought to verify it. TriMet provided documentation to support the statistic, which involved analyzing data from traffic-counting stations and MAX ridership.

To determine the number of commuters using the MAX, TriMet examined the average ridership for a weekday between 4:30 and 5:30 p.m. at two MAX stations: Lloyd Center on the Banfield freeway and Goose Hollow on the Sunset freeway. The agency found that approximately 2,200 riders traveled eastbound and 1,600 riders traveled westbound during this time period.

Counting the number of vehicles passing through the freeways proved to be more complex, but TriMet was able to obtain data from the Oregon Department of Transportation's traffic-counting system, which is housed at Portland State University. The agency used this data to estimate the average number of commuters per vehicle.

To make this comparison, TriMet relied on a study by the Federal Highway Administration, which reported that the average number of commuters in a vehicle is approximately 1.13. By applying this figure to the traffic-counting data, TriMet estimated that about 4,600 commuters traveled eastbound by car and approximately 4,400 traveled westbound.

When compared to the MAX ridership figures, the data supported TriMet's claim that approximately 30 percent of evening commuters along the Banfield and Sunset highways use the MAX. This figure is slightly lower for the morning commute.

One potential concern was that the 1.13 passengers per car figure used by TriMet might not be representative of Portland's commuting habits, given the city's high rate of bike commuting and carpooling. However, a review of Census data from the American Community Survey suggests that Portland's carpooling rate is in line with the national average, which may support the use of the 1.13 figure.

In conclusion, TriMet's claim that the MAX carries 30 percent of evening rush hour commuters traveling from Downtown on the Sunset and Banfield freeways is supported by reliable data and appears to be accurate.

We rate this statement True.

Editor's Note: This article was originally published on October 11, 2011, in conjunction with a Republican presidential primary debate in New Hampshire. We initially rated a statement made by Rep. Michele Bachmann as True, citing similar claims made by other politicians, including Florida Senator Marco Rubio and North Dakota Senator Kent Conrad. However, an alert reader pointed out a discrepancy in our calculation, prompting us to re-examine Bachmann's statement.

The U.S. government is facing a significant fiscal challenge, with its spending exceeding its revenues and relying on borrowing to maintain its operations.

During a Republican presidential debate on October 11, 2011, at Dartmouth College in Hanover, N.H., Rep. Michele Bachmann stated, "Our government right now -- this is significant -- we are spending 40 percent more than what we take in."

To assess the accuracy of Bachmann's claim, we consulted the Congressional Budget Office's (CBO) preliminary figures for Fiscal Year 2011, which ended September 30. According to the CBO's data, the federal government had revenues of $2.3 trillion and expenditures of $3.6 trillion, resulting in a deficit of $1.3 trillion.

To calculate the percentage by which expenditures exceeded revenues, we divided $3.6 trillion by $2.3 trillion, arriving at a figure of approximately 56 percent. This calculation was verified by two experts from the conservative Heritage Foundation and the left-leaning Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.

In response to our inquiry, Bachmann's campaign did not provide a statement. However, it appears that she may have misstated a figure that has been cited by other politicians in recent months.

For example, Senator Kent Conrad (D-N.D.) stated in January 2011, "We're borrowing 40 cents of every dollar we spend." Similarly, Scott Rigell, a Republican representative from Virginia's Second District, said in a February 2011 press release, "We are a nation $14 trillion in debt and are borrowing more than 40 cents of every dollar we spend." However, these statements refer to the proportions of spending funded by taxes versus borrowing, rather than the ratio of expenditures to revenues.

Our analysis indicates that Bachmann's claim was actually an underestimation, as the correct percentage by which federal spending exceeded revenues in 2011 was 56 percent, not 40. Nevertheless, her broader point about the government's fiscal situation remains accurate. We maintain our initial rating of True for Bachmann's statement.

The video ends with the words "IRAQ WITHDRAWAL DATE: 12,008.... GOOD LUCK WITH THAT IN NOVEMBER."

Senator Barack Obama made a similar charge during the Democratic debate in Cleveland, Ohio, on February 26, 2008, when he said, "We are bogged down in a war that John McCain now suggests might go on for another 100 years." However, this statement was not entirely accurate.

To understand the context of McCain's remarks, it is essential to examine his previous statements on the matter. At a town hall meeting in Derry, New Hampshire, on January 3, 2008, McCain was asked about the potential duration of a U.S. presence in Iraq. He replied, "Make it a hundred" when asked about President Bush's suggestion of a 50-year presence. McCain later clarified that he was referring to a peacetime presence, not the war.

In subsequent interviews, McCain elaborated on his position, stating that he expects the United States could have troops in Iraq similar to the presence in South Korea and Germany. He emphasized that the key factor is not the duration of the presence, but rather the level of American casualties. McCain said, "If Americans are there in a support role, but they're not taking casualties, that's fine."

When asked about the potential duration of a U.S. presence in Iraq on ABC's Good Morning America on January 9, 2008, McCain said, "Could be 1,000 years or a million years." However, this statement was not meant to imply that the war would continue for that long. Rather, McCain was highlighting the long-term commitment of the United States to maintaining a presence in certain regions, such as South Korea and Germany.

The interviews show that McCain is not advocating for a prolonged war in Iraq. Instead, he is suggesting that the United States could maintain a peacetime presence in Iraq, similar to its presence in other regions, for an extended period.

In conclusion, the videos and Obama's statement made during the Democratic debate were not entirely accurate representations of McCain's comments. While McCain did suggest that a U.S. presence in Iraq could last for many years, he was referring to a peacetime presence, not the war.

Sarah Palin Reiterates Claim on End-of-Life Counseling in Health Care Bill

Former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin has again taken to her Facebook page to address criticism surrounding her claims that the proposed health care reform bill would create "death panels." Palin argues that end-of-life counseling authorized in the House version of the health plan is not entirely voluntary.

This claim has been previously disputed by experts, including Betsy McCaughey, former lieutenant governor of New York, who stated that the bill would require Medicare patients to undergo end-of-life counseling sessions every five years. However, several health care experts have countered that the bill would make the counseling available but voluntary.

The House bill, specifically Section 1233, authorizes advanced care planning consultations for senior citizens on Medicare every five years, or more often if there is a significant change in their health condition. During these consultations, practitioners must explain the continuum of end-of-life services and supports available, including palliative care and hospice, and the government benefits available to pay for such services.

Palin argues that this provision must be viewed in the context of a health care bill aimed at reducing health care spending. She suggests that senior citizens might view such consultations as attempts to convince them to accept minimal end-of-life care to reduce costs.

However, experts, including Jim Dau, national spokesman for AARP, and Dr. Gail Wilensky, a health care policy researcher, have confirmed that the end-of-life counseling sessions in the House bill are voluntary. Wilensky stated that the legislation ensures that people can determine their own fate and have the conversation with their physicians and families when they are not under physical or emotional duress.

In her Facebook post, Palin also cited an opinion piece by Charles Lane of the Washington Post, which suggests that the consultations envisioned in Section 1233 are not purely voluntary. Florida Felons Face Long Road to Regaining Voting Rights

A proposed constitutional amendment in Florida aims to automatically restore voting rights to felons who have completed their sentences. The effort is led by Desmond Meade, a convicted drug offender who graduated from law school and now serves as the president of the Florida Rights Restoration Coalition.

Meade's advocacy for voting rights reform gained national attention after comedian Samantha Bee featured him on her TBS show, Full Frontal, in May. Bee highlighted the issue of felons struggling to regain civil rights in Florida, a state where 1.68 million felons have lost the right to vote.

According to Meade, Florida's voting rights restoration process is overly restrictive, with many felons facing a lengthy and cumbersome process to regain their rights. The Florida Constitution states that individuals convicted of felonies are not qualified to vote or hold office until their civil rights are restored.

Research has shown that restoration of rights for felons is a hot topic in Florida, a swing state where changes to the voting population can have a significant impact. In some states, more felons have registered as Democrats than Republicans after being released from prison.

The proposed amendment, which was unanimously approved by the Florida Supreme Court in April, would automatically restore voting rights to felons who have completed their sentences, including parole or probation. However, felons convicted of murder or sexual offenses would still need to petition the Florida Cabinet and governor for restoration.

Meade, a recovered drug addict who served three years in prison for a 2001 firearm possession charge, is among the felons who have lost their civil rights. He and other advocates are working to collect the required 700,000 signatures to place the question on the ballot in 2018.

While the Florida Constitution broadly applies to all types of felonies, experts note that the process of restoring rights is often lengthy and difficult. Between 2011 and April 2017, about 2,600 felons had their rights restored, while over 10,000 cases were pending.

The proposed amendment aims to address the issue of automatic restoration of voting rights for felons, which is currently a lengthy and cumbersome process. The amendment would not apply to felons convicted of murder or sexual offenses, who would still need to petition the Florida Cabinet and governor for restoration.

Meade's claim that individuals could lose their rights for life over something as simple as driving with a suspended license is mostly true, according to PolitiFact. While the first and second convictions for driving with a suspended license are misdemeanors, a third or subsequent conviction is a third-degree felony, which can result in the loss of voting rights.

The Syrian Civil War and Refugee Crisis: A Debate at the United Nations

The ongoing Syrian civil war has led to a significant refugee crisis, prompting debate at the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York last month. Several countries remain cautious about accepting refugees from the Middle East, citing concerns that some may be terrorists or criminals.

At the Leader's Summit on Refugees on September 20, President Barack Obama addressed these concerns in a speech, emphasizing the need for increased humanitarian aid to conflict zones and a fair share of refugees. He argued that refugees are subject to rigorous screening and security checks before being allowed to enter the United States.

"In recent years, in the United States, we've implemented intensive screening and security checks to ensure the safety of our citizens," Obama said. "In fact, refugees undergo more rigorous screening than the average tourist."

Government officials have made similar statements, noting that refugees are subject to the most comprehensive screening process of any visitors to the United States.

However, some politicians, such as Donald Trump, have raised doubts about the government's ability to vet refugees and ensure they do not pose a threat to the country. To examine the validity of Obama's claim, a comparison of the screening processes for tourists and refugees was conducted.

Comparing Tourist and Refugee Screening Protocols

The Department of Homeland Security's official protocols for tourist and refugee screening were examined, outlining the key components of each process.

Tourists from 38 countries, including the United Kingdom, Australia, and Japan, can apply for the visa waiver program, which allows them to visit the United States for up to 90 days without a visa. Applicants must have passports with security features and obtain approval through the Electronic System for Travel Authorization.

Visitors who do not apply for the visa waiver program must apply for a visitor's visa, requiring a valid passport, resume, and photo ID to complete the DS-160 online application. They must also pass a visa interview, where they may be asked to provide evidence of their trip's purpose.

In contrast, the refugee screening process is more complex and time-consuming, often taking at least two years to complete. Refugees are first identified, assessed, and interviewed by the United Nations' refugee agency, UNHCR. They then undergo a strict screening process while overseas, involving security checks and interviews with multiple federal agencies.

Refugees must also pass medical screenings, attend cultural orientation classes, and have their fingerprints cross-referenced against terrorist watch lists. Those from Syria face additional security checks and may be referred to fraud detection experts in Homeland Security.

Experts Weigh In

David Martin, a professor of law at the University of Virginia, confirmed that Obama's statement is accurate, noting that the refugee screening process is strictly enforced and more rigorous than the tourist screening process.

However, Martin acknowledged that no security screening is foolproof, and the lack of access to government data in war-torn countries can make it difficult to verify individuals' identities.

Anne Speckhard, an associate professor of psychiatry at Georgetown University, expressed concerns about the relative laxity of the visa waiver program, which she believes poses a greater risk of allowing terrorists to enter the United States.

Matt Mayer of the American Enterprise Institute argued that Obama's comparison between refugees and tourists is flawed, as refugees are coming to the United States permanently, whereas tourists visit briefly. Mayer emphasized the need for extensive screening due to widespread problems with document fraud and verifying individuals' identities.

Conclusion

Reviewing the government's vetting protocols confirms that refugees face a more rigorous and lengthy screening process than tourists for entering the United States. Experts consulted agreed that the refugee protocol is strictly enforced and more difficult than the tourist screening process.

Therefore, we rate Obama's claim as True.

Wisconsin Tea Party Leader Alleges Democrats Harassed Recall Petition Signers

A controversy has emerged in Wisconsin over the recall petition process, with a local tea party leader accusing the state's Democratic Party of harassing individuals who signed recall petitions against a Democratic senator.

Kim Simac, a Wisconsin tea party leader and founder of the Northwoods Patriots, claimed that petition signers were subjected to harassing phone calls from out-of-state telemarketers claiming to represent the Democratic Party and insinuating foul play by petition circulators. The allegations were made in a news release issued eight days after Simac submitted over 23,000 signatures to the Government Accountability Board in support of a recall election against state Sen. Jim Holperin.

Holperin, a Democrat who represents a North Woods district, had fled to Illinois in February 2011, along with 13 other Democratic senators, to delay a vote on Republican Gov. Scott Walker's budget-repair bill. The bill, which curtails the collective bargaining power of most state and local government employees, eventually became law despite court challenges that have kept the collective bargaining changes from taking effect.

The recall movement, which was sparked by the law and the Democrats' reaction to it, led to campaigns against all 16 state senators eligible for recall. Simac, who headed the signature-collecting campaign to recall Holperin, announced plans to run against him if a recall election is set.

In response to Simac's allegations, Holperin stated that he authorized the Wisconsin Democratic Party to call about 5,000 of the people who signed recall petitions against him. According to Holperin, the calls were made to address concerns about the legitimacy of the petitions, which were collected by both volunteer circulators and paid staff from a Colorado marketing and consulting firm hired by the Wisconsin Republican Party.

An investigation by PolitiFact Wisconsin found that many of the people who received the calls reported being asked if they understood what they had signed and whether they were aware of the purpose of the petition. Some callers also stated that reports had been received that out-of-state paid circulators were misleading people about what they were being asked to sign.

PolitiFact Wisconsin interviewed 10 individuals who received the calls and found that while some people felt harassed by the calls, others did not. The callers were employed by an out-of-state firm and identified themselves as representing the Wisconsin Democratic Party.

In response to allegations that the Democratic Party was insinuating foul play by petition circulators, Holperin provided a script used by the telemarketing firm, which showed that callers were instructed to ask people if they were aware of the purpose of the petition and to state that reports had been received of out-of-state paid circulators misleading people.

PolitiFact Wisconsin rates Simac's claim as True, as evidence supports the fact that petition signers received calls from out-of-state telemarketers claiming to represent the Democratic Party and insinuating foul play by petition circulators.

The Role of Religion in the Arkansas Senate Race: A Complex Issue

In the 2014 Arkansas Senate campaign, the role of religion has become a significant factor, particularly in relation to the Employment Non-Discrimination Act (ENDA). Incumbent Senator Mark Pryor, a Democrat, recently released an ad highlighting the Bible's influence on his decision-making. However, his stance on ENDA has drawn criticism from the National Republican Senatorial Committee, which has accused Pryor of contradicting his Christian values.

Interestingly, Pryor's challenger, Representative Tom Cotton, has distanced himself from the National Republican Senatorial Committee's attack, instead choosing to support Pryor's position on ENDA. The issue has sparked a debate among lawmakers, advocacy groups, and religious leaders, with some arguing that ENDA discriminates against Christian organizations.

The Traditional Values Coalition, a conservative religious group, has criticized Pryor for his vote in favor of ENDA, claiming that the bill discriminates against Christian daycare centers, parents, business owners, and the rights of religious freedom. However, a closer examination of the bill reveals that it includes a broad religious exemption, which would allow churches and other religious institutions to discriminate based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

American Christianity and LGBT Rights

Within Christianity, the issue of gay rights is a complex and divisive topic. While some Christian groups, such as the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, oppose ENDA, others, like ReconcilingWorks, a Lutheran organization that welcomes LGBT members, support the bill. According to Kate Bowler, a professor of American Christianity at Duke University, there is a growing trend of Christians accepting same-sex unions.

ENDA Basics

The Employment Non-Discrimination Act would prohibit private-sector employers and government employers from discriminating against employees based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The bill includes a broad religious exemption, which would exempt churches and other religious institutions from complying with the law. Additionally, businesses with fewer than 15 employees would be exempt from the law, regardless of their religious affiliation.

Experts Weigh In

Law professors and experts in religious liberty have weighed in on the Traditional Values Coalition's claim that ENDA discriminates against Christians. According to Nelson Tebbe, a professor at Brooklyn Law School, ENDA's religious exemption exceeds that of the Civil Rights Act of 1964's Title VII. The exemption would allow religious organizations to discriminate based on sexual orientation and gender identity, whereas Title VII only permits discrimination based on religion.

Breakdown of the Traditional Values Coalition's Claim

The Traditional Values Coalition has claimed that ENDA discriminates against Christian daycare centers, parents, business owners, and the rights of religious freedom. However, experts have disputed this claim, pointing out that the bill's religious exemption would apply to any religion, not just Christianity. Additionally, the bill would not require parents to alter their beliefs or teaching practices, and for-profit companies with 15 employees or more would need to comply with the law.

Conclusion

The debate over ENDA has highlighted the complex and often contentious relationship between religion and LGBT rights. While some Christians may take issue with the bill, the language used by the Traditional Values Coalition is too broad and overstated. Our analysis indicates that ENDA does not discriminate against Christians, but rather provides a broad religious exemption that applies to any religion. Therefore, we rate the Traditional Values Coalition's claim as False.

In 2007, the year Sink took office, the pension was worth $136.3 billion, and in 2010, her last year as CFO, the value had decreased to $109.3 billion. This represents a net loss of $27 billion, as claimed by the Republican Party.

This claim echoes criticisms made by the party during Sink's 2010 gubernatorial campaign against Rick Scott. However, there are several important caveats to consider.

The comparison of pension values at different points in history may not be as severe as it seems. There is no permanent loss in value until the assets are sold. Although the pension's value was temporarily lower in 2010 than in 2007, the funds are not irretrievable.

**The Devastating Truth Behind Wisconsin's Surplus: A Nation's Recovery in Shambles**

As Governor Scott Walker proudly boasts about Wisconsin's $1 billion surplus, the harsh reality is that this financial windfall is built on the backs of the middle class. The Democratic Party of Wisconsin is speaking out against Walker's claim, revealing the dark truth behind the state's newfound wealth.

Walker's belt-tightening measures, tax cuts, and business-friendly deregulation have come at a devastating cost to the state's public schools and technical college system. By slashing nearly $1 billion from these vital institutions, Walker has left the economic security of the middle class hanging by a thread.

But Wisconsin is not alone in its struggle. The national economic recovery has been a double-edged sword, bringing higher-than-expected tax revenues and projected budget surpluses to nearly every state in the nation. The nonpartisan Legislative Fiscal Bureau has confirmed that Wisconsin's surplus is largely due to rising tax collections, a trend that is being mirrored across the country.

In fact, the National Association of State Budget Officers (NASBO) has reported that almost all states will see fairly decent surpluses in their 2014 budgets. This is not a result of prudent financial decisions, but rather a one-time windfall from the 2013 stock market surge. Many states had budgeted conservatively for 2014, not anticipating the market's runup.

The revenue windfalls have meant surpluses are common, with 37 states exceeding original revenue forecasts in 2013. The National Conference of State Legislatures has also confirmed that state fiscal conditions continued to improve in 2013, with general fund revenue growth outpacing projections in most states.

But the reality is that these surpluses are not a sustainable solution to the state's financial woes. Many states are using the excess to supplement appropriations or fortify their rainy day funds, rather than addressing the underlying issues that led to the budget shortfalls in the first place.

The Democratic Party of Wisconsin's claim that the national economic recovery has led to higher-than-expected tax revenues and projected budget surpluses in nearly every state in the nation, including Wisconsin, is a harsh reminder of the devastating consequences of Walker's policies. This fiscal year may not match 2013 in tax-revenue growth, but the damage has already been done.
